ideas.title: Deferred-Payment Shield for Grain Sellers
ideas.one_liner: A counterparty-risk monitor plus surety/letter-of-credit wrap that turns the unsecured December 'deferred payment' loans farmers unknowingly make to their elevators into protected receivables.
ideas.customer: Row-crop operators with 2,000+ acres who each defer $400k to $2M of grain revenue into January, and the ag lenders and farm CPAs who advise them. Co-ops and elevators with strong balance sheets are a secondary payer, because the wrap becomes a way to win bushels.
ideas.problem: Every November and December, farmers sign deferred payment contracts to push income into next year for tax reasons. Most think they are just delaying a check. Legally, title has passed and they are unsecured creditors of the buyer. Iowa's Grain Indemnity Fund gives deferred payment contracts zero coverage. Deferred pricing ('price later') contracts get 75% coverage capped at $400,000 per claimant. Farm balance sheets are stretched, so more farmers are lending large sums to buyers they have never vetted.
ideas.solution: Start with a free 'Elevator Exposure Report'. The farmer lists every open contract, prepaid input balance and stored-grain receipt. The tool compares total exposure with the Fund's actual coverage and scores each buyer using licensing status, audit history, buyer size, and settlement-timing behavior reported by users. Then sell the fix. A specialty MGA or bank issues a surety bond or standby letter of credit against the buyer's payment promise, structured with ag tax counsel so tax deferral is preserved. The fee is roughly 0.3% to 0.8% of face value. Ag lenders subscribe to a portfolio dashboard showing how much of their borrowers' grain receivables sit with weak buyers.
ideas.why_now: Chapter 12 farm bankruptcies rose 46% in 2025 and April 2026 hit a six-year high. USDA projects record farm debt of about $625B in 2026. The 2025 bumper crop and low prices pushed farmers toward deferral and storage. The 2026 December deferral season opens in about 90 days, which is a hard deadline for a first pilot.
ideas.revenue_model: Wrap fee split with the surety or LC provider (0.3% to 0.8% of contract face value). Ag lender portfolio-monitoring subscription ($1k to $5k a month per lender). Optional $299 per farm annual exposure audit sold through CPAs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The elevator that pushes deferred payment contracts hardest in November is often the one that needs your cash, because deferrals are free working capital for a thinly capitalized buyer. Farmers think of the elevator as a warehouse. Once title passes, it is a borrower. Nobody rates that borrower.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the exposure calculator as a free web form and scorecard from Iowa Dept. of Ag license data and public filings. Get 5 farm CPAs and 3 rural banks to run their biggest clients through it. Sign one surety broker or bank willing to quote wraps, and target 10 paid wraps before the December deferral rush.

ideas.title: Farm Income Dial: ACA Cliff Management
ideas.one_liner: A December planning service that uses the grain-contract and input-prepay levers farmers already control to keep household income under the 400% poverty cliff and avoid repaying a full year of health subsidies.
ideas.customer: Farm families who buy ACA marketplace coverage. KFF estimates about 27% of farmers do, nearly triple the adult average. The co-op grain desks and rural CPA firms that advise them pay for a white-label version.
ideas.problem: The enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, so the hard cutoff at 400% of poverty is back (roughly $130k for a family of four). The 2025 tax law also removed repayment caps for tax year 2026. A farm family that projected income under the line and then lands $2,000 over must repay every dollar of advance credits, often $15k to $25k. Farm income is lumpy and depends on prices and yields nobody knows in January. Farm CPAs optimize the federal tax bracket, not the ACA cliff, and nobody connects the two.
ideas.solution: Farmers connect their grain settlements, deferred contracts, prepaid inputs and equipment purchases. The tool tracks estimated 2026 MAGI against the cliff and gives a concrete action list: how many bushels to defer into 2027, how much fertilizer to prepay, when to elect CCC loan treatment, when to buy equipment. It also models plan choice for 2027 open enrollment, including Farm Bureau non-ACA plans and their underwriting risks. Every recommendation is reviewed by the household's CPA, so this is planning software and not tax advice.
ideas.why_now: This is the first tax year with no repayment cap and no enhanced credits. Marketplace enrollment fell from 22.1M to 19.2M in a year. The planning window closes December 31, 2026, and every Iowa farm family on a marketplace plan is exposed right now.
ideas.revenue_model: $350 to $600 per farm household per season. Broker commissions from carriers when the tool places 2027 coverage. White-label licenses to rural CPA firms and co-op grain desks ($50 to $100 per client). Optional success fee of 10% of the protected credit.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The ACA cliff is controlled with the same pen that signs deferred-payment contracts. The co-op grain desk is the real MAGI control panel for farm families. CPAs do not see it because they only meet clients in February, after the levers are gone.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2 rural CPA firms and one co-op grain desk. Build a spreadsheet-grade calculator plus a one-page 'cliff letter' for clients. Run a 'Cliff Night' at the co-op with farm families in October and November. Convert 30 to 50 households at $350 before the December deadline and document dollars saved.

ideas.title: Co-op Ledger Signals: Farm Distress Early Warning
ideas.one_liner: Benchmark co-ops on their own receivables, then sell the anonymized, county-level 'who is paying whom first' data to lenders, insurers and equipment financiers as a leading indicator of farm distress.
ideas.customer: First payers: co-op managers and CFOs, who buy the benchmark dashboard. Data buyers: Farmer Mac, Farm Credit institutions, regional ag banks, equipment captive finance arms, input manufacturers, ag reinsurers and funds trading farm-exposed equities.
ideas.problem: Ag bank delinquency stats and Fed surveys lag reality by two to three quarters. Meanwhile every co-op ERP quietly holds the earliest signal: accounts-receivable aging by customer, the timing of input payments, and who is asking for deferred-payment or extended-terms deals. Farmers in trouble pay in a predictable order (operating lender, landlord, seed, then the co-op), so slow co-op payments show up long before defaults. Each co-op sees only its own trade area and cannot tell whether its collection problems are local or systemic.
ideas.solution: Ship a free-to-cheap benchmark: connect the co-op's grain and ag-retail accounting system (Agvance, Agris and similar) and get peer comparisons on A/R over 90 days, prepay behavior, and credit-line usage. In return, contribute anonymized data to a pooled index with strict privacy rules (a minimum of 5 co-ops per cell, county-by-month, no farmer-level data). Sell the county-level Farm Payment Stress Index to lenders and funds, with a second SKU for weekly harvest-pace and grain-quality metrics (moisture, test weight, damage) from scale tickets. Co-ops receive a revenue share.
ideas.why_now: Chapter 12 filings are up sharply, the Chicago Fed reports rising loan rollovers and falling cash rents, and USDA projects record farm debt. Federal data proved brittle during the fall 2025 shutdown, and lenders and funds want independent ground truth without waiting for quarterly surveys.
ideas.revenue_model: Co-op benchmark subscription ($300 to $800 a month). Index licenses to lenders and reinsurers ($25k to $150k a year). Fund data feeds ($5k to $15k a month). Co-ops receive 40% to 50% of data revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The co-op's boring back-office ledger is the best real-time farm-distress sensor in America. Co-op managers think the data is too mundane to sell. The way to get it is to give them the peer benchmark they have always wanted and only then aggregate.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 to 8 co-ops through state co-op councils and CFO peer groups with a free 'A/R health check'. Build an ETL for the two or three most common co-op ERPs. Produce the first county-level index by Q4 2026. Pitch two ag lenders and one reinsurer for paid pilots.

ideas.title: Orphan Bin Network: Leased Farm Storage Capacity
ideas.one_liner: Lease the thousands of idle grain bins left on consolidated and inherited farmsteads, retrofit them with cheap sensors, and run them as licensed satellite storage for co-ops.
ideas.customer: Co-ops and independent elevators that run short of upright storage every big harvest. Also landlord and heir bin owners who receive lease income. The elevator pays a per-bin SaaS fee plus a share of storage revenue.
ideas.problem: Upright storage is the co-op's hardest constraint, and building new capacity costs a huge multiple of leasing existing steel. Ground piles cost shrink and quality. Meanwhile farm consolidation and aging landowners leave many bins idle on rented farmsteads. Heirs pay taxes on stranded assets and have no way to monetize them. Iowa law already contemplates leased storage facilities under a warehouse license (the licensee simply notifies the state), but no one has packaged the monitoring, inventory verification and paperwork to make it routine.
ideas.solution: A 'bin-in-a-box' program run under the co-op's existing warehouse license. Sign multi-year leases with owners and install a retrofit kit: temperature and moisture cables, fill-level sensors, aeration control and a remote camera. Wire it into the co-op's grain accounting system so receipts, inventory and shrink tracking work like any owned bin. Provide the compliance package (state notifications, insurance riders, inspection logs, an auditor-ready trail). This is not a marketplace. The co-op stays the licensed warehouseman and the bin owner becomes a landlord.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 record harvest left the top 12 corn states about 1.4 billion bushels short of upright storage, according to CoBank analysis, and low prices keep grain in storage longer. Elevators piled grain on the ground and rented temporary space. Cheap LoRa and cellular bin sensors now cost far less than a few years ago, and 2026 harvest is starting.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS of about $250 to $500 per bin per year plus install margin on the sensor kit. 10% to 20% share of incremental storage revenue. Optional financing spread on kit costs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not steel but licensed, monitored, insurable steel. Idle bins already exist by the thousands. What is missing is the trust layer (sensors, chain-of-custody and a bonded warehouseman) that lets an elevator sign for grain sitting in someone else's yard.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one co-op that just piled grain on the ground. Identify 10 idle bins within 15 miles from the co-op's landlord and ag-lending contacts. Confirm the notification steps with the Iowa Grain Warehouse Bureau. Install sensor kits on 5 bins before harvest peak and store real grain for the first time this season.

ideas.title: RouteRx: Pharmacy Delivery on Co-op Fuel Routes
ideas.one_liner: Piggyback prescription and essentials delivery onto the propane, fuel and feed routes that already pass most rural households, so surviving independent pharmacies can serve people the chains just abandoned.
ideas.customer: Independent rural pharmacies (per-delivery fee), Medicare Advantage and Part D plans and rural health clinics (per-member adherence and wellness-check fee), and the co-op energy department, which keeps a share of route revenue.
ideas.problem: Rite Aid is gone, Walgreens is closing about 1,200 stores through 2027, and more than 2,000 US pharmacies closed in 2025 alone. Rural residents, especially older ones on propane and well water, are hours from a counter. Standalone courier delivery in a county of 12,000 people costs $15 to $30 a drop in deadhead miles. Independents cannot afford it, and plans cannot buy adherence in places with no last mile.
ideas.solution: The co-op's energy drivers already pass nearly every farmstead and acreage in a 25-mile radius on weekly or monthly cycles. They know the gate codes, where the dog is, and which customers live alone. Add a locked, tamper-evident tote and a driver app with signature capture and temperature logging. A partner pharmacy dispenses, and the driver acts as its contracted courier under existing Iowa delivery rules, with no controlled substances at first. Add optional 'no-heat and welfare check' notes that flag when a propane customer looks unwell, triggering a call to family or the clinic.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 to 2026 pharmacy shakeout has left rural pharmacy deserts, and Drug Channels' August 2026 analysis describes a K-shaped market of urban consolidation and rural lost access. Payers are looking for adherence and social-needs benefits. Co-op energy departments are under margin pressure and need new route revenue.
ideas.revenue_model: $5 to $9 per delivery from pharmacies. Medicare Advantage and Part D plan per-member-per-month adherence and check-in fees. The co-op takes a route revenue share of roughly 30%. Optional expansion to labs, groceries and parcels.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in rural health is not delivery technology but route density that is already paid for. A propane bobtail passing a home every three weeks has a near-zero marginal stop cost, and it carries something no courier startup has, which is trust from decades of showing up.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one co-op with an LP fleet and one independent pharmacy in an adjacent town that just lost a competitor. Get a written read from the Iowa Board of Pharmacy and the co-op's insurer. Run a 20-household pilot with tamper-evident bags and an off-the-shelf delivery app. Record cost per stop and refill adherence to pitch a regional Medicare Advantage plan.

ideas.title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Dead Importers
ideas.one_liner: A contingency service that finds failed or dormant importers whose IEEPA refund claims are stranded, revives them or works through their bankruptcy trustee, and files the claims through a licensed broker.
ideas.customer: Chapter 7 trustees and ABC assignees of failed importers, plus founders of dissolved or dormant small importers. They pay 20-30% of recovered dollars. Secondary customers are claim buyers who want vetted entry-level claim files.
ideas.problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP is now refunding through CAPE in phases: Phase 1 opened Apr 20 for unliquidated and recently liquidated entries, Phase 2 came in June, and Phase 3 (late July) covers finally liquidated entries only for importers who sued at the CIT. Refunds go to the importer of record (or the broker who filed the entry). Every entry has its own clock, including the 180-day protest window. A large tail of small importers closed or went dark during the 2025 tariff shock. Their refunds are six-figure receivables spread across hundreds of ACE entries. They appear on nobody's balance sheet, and nobody at the dead company is watching for them. A trustee liquidating the estate usually does not know the asset exists.
ideas.solution: Build an entry-level refund estimator from public bill-of-lading data, HTS lines, country of origin and the IEEPA rate schedule. Cross-match importer names against state dissolution lists and PACER filings to rank stranded claims by likely dollar value. Then run the recovery: (1) approach trustees with an asset-discovery letter and a court-approvable contingency engagement; (2) for dissolved entities, reinstate the corporation under state law, re-enroll ACH, and file CF-4811 designations where needed; (3) have a licensed broker file CAPE declarations for the entries that broker filed; (4) send finally liquidated entries to partner trade counsel for CIT reliquidation orders under the July 17 order. The moat is a licensed-broker partner plus a pipeline of claims that nobody else is hunting.
ideas.why_now: IEEPA was struck down Feb 20, 2026. CAPE phases rolled out Apr-Jul 2026, and the July 17 CIT order created a court-driven Phase 3. Per-entry deadlines are now running. Existing refund tools (deadline trackers and CAPE filing helpers) all sell to living importers who are already paying attention. Nobody productized the orphaned-claim hunt.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on refunds recovered, plus interest. Trustee engagements are approved by the bankruptcy court as contingency fee arrangements. A secondary line sells diligenced claim packages to claim buyers at a flat fee per package.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The refund is attached to the importer-of-record number, not to whoever was actually hurt, and only the IOR or the filing broker can claim it in the early phases. Brokers hold the entry data but their powers of attorney die with the client, and chasing a dead client is unbillable work, so nobody does it. A broker can still file CAPE for entries it filed, which makes the broker the key that unlocks these claims. Outsiders see the refund as a tax-accounting topic. Insiders see it as an unclaimed-property hunt across ACE.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: pull 2025 importer-level volumes for China, Vietnam, India and other tariffed origins from ImportYeti or a cheap paid BOL feed, then estimate each importer's IEEPA duty. Week 2: cross-match against CA, NY, TX, FL and NJ dissolution records and PACER chapter 7 and ABC filings, and rank the top 150 targets above about $50k. Week 3: send trustees a one-page asset-discovery letter, since trustee contact info is public, and have a trade lawyer draft the contingency engagement. Week 4: sign the first 3-5 estates, or dormant founders, and file the first CAPE declarations through the partner broker.

ideas.title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
ideas.one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
ideas.customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
ideas.problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
ideas.solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
ideas.why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
ideas.revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.

ideas.title: Customs-Verified Collateral for Inventory Lenders
ideas.one_liner: An API and reporting layer that verifies borrowers' in-transit inventory against ISF, entry, release and liquidation records, so lenders stop financing containers that do not exist.
ideas.customer: Inventory-finance and revenue-based lenders for e-commerce brands, factoring companies, ABL desks at small banks, and buyers of tariff-refund receivables. They pay per verification and per monitored loan.
ideas.problem: Lenders finance purchase orders and goods on the water. Their collateral evidence is invoices, a bill of lading PDF and the borrower's word. Fraud, double-pledging, inflated quantities and phantom shipments are a chronic loss driver in small-business trade finance. Tariffs made it worse: duties now consume a big share of landed cost, so lenders need to know what was actually declared, at what value, and whether it cleared or is held. The truth exists in CBP data that brokers see within hours. Lenders see it, if at all, weeks late through the borrower.
ideas.solution: Connect to the collateral through consent-based data paths: importer-scheduled ACE reports forwarded to a dedicated inbox, and ABI/status feeds from cooperating brokers that get paid for sharing. Reconcile each financed PO against ISF filing, entry summary, release or hold status, declared value and HTS, and (after the IEEPA ruling) refund eligibility. Deliver a loan-level 'entry-verified' status and exception alerts, such as a container that never had an ISF, a value mismatch, or an exam hold that makes collateral illiquid. The same engine verifies IEEPA refund claims for lenders advancing against them.
ideas.why_now: Inventory financing and tariff-duty financing for e-commerce brands surged in 2024-26, and lenders are absorbing losses they do not yet understand. Refund-backed lending is new since the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling and CAPE, and it needs entry-level verification. ACE reports are self-serve, so no permission from CBP is needed. Brokers are looking for revenue beyond thin filing fees.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40 per shipment verification, or a monitoring SaaS fee of about 5-15 basis points on funded volume, with platform minimums of $2-5k a month. Brokers get a revenue share on data feeds. Add-on: refund-claim diligence packages.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A PO and a bill of lading are easy to forge. An ISF filed before vessel loading, tied to a bond, followed by a release message from CBP, is not. It is the closest thing to a government-attested proof that goods exist and are moving. Because the importer owns the ACE data, no data-broker licensing fight is needed. Trade-finance software vendors model documents. Nobody models the entry record.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach five small inventory lenders, factors and refund-claim buyers with a manual pilot: they send 10 borrowers' entry data, and you return verified and unverified lists within 48 hours. Recruit two friendly customs brokers for feed access on consenting clients. Build the reconciliation on spreadsheets and scripts first, and charge $500-$1,500 per pilot batch. The first paid lender contract is usually a covenant addition: 'borrower must forward ACE reports monthly'.

ideas.title: Distressed Cargo Rescue Desk for Bankrupt Importers
ideas.one_liner: A broker-run desk that takes orphaned containers from failed importers, clears the four-way legal tangle in days, and delivers the goods to off-price buyers at deep discounts.
ideas.customer: Off-price retailers, closeout buyers and liquidators who cannot currently buy orphaned cargo because they are not the consignee. Carriers and CFS operators, who want the boxes gone, and trustees, who want recovery, are the supply side. The buyer pays a handling fee or a spread.
ideas.problem: When a small importer fails mid-shipment, the goods sit on the water or on a terminal with no ISF, no entry, no bond and a demurrage and storage clock running. The bills of lading are in a dead company's name. Carriers and warehouses will not release cargo to strangers. Buyers would pay well for the goods but cannot make entry. Unentered cargo can be sent to a General Order warehouse after about 15 days and is subject to public sale after roughly six months, so value bleeds out. Many boxes are eventually abandoned, auctioned for pennies or destroyed. The 2025-26 tariff whiplash left a long tail of failed importers, and Long Beach's record volumes keep yard space and free time expensive.
ideas.solution: Run a cargo rescue desk with five steps. (1) Source: call carriers' demurrage collection desks, CFS warehouses in Carson and Long Beach, and bankruptcy trustees to find orphaned cargo. (2) Screen: triage compliance risk (CPSC certification, FDA, FCC, UFLPA and IPR issues) and refuse any box that cannot be legally sold. (3) Title: obtain the trustee's or owner's transfer of cargo rights and a negotiated carrier release, trading the removal of the box for a waiver or reduction of demurrage. (4) Entry: the purchaser, as an actual purchaser with the right to make entry, becomes importer of record on a single-transaction bond, with a licensed broker filing the entry. (5) Deliver to the buyer's warehouse. Where the invoices are non-compliant, a dispute of the demurrage under the FMC's billing rules adds leverage.
ideas.why_now: Small-brand failures peaked through the 2025 tariff shock and its aftershocks. The IEEPA reversal of Feb 2026 has estates now holding refund cash but still holding stranded physical goods. Off-price retail demand for cheap inventory is high. Single-transaction customs bonds mean a new team does not need a continuous bond or big capital to start.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-15% handling and sourcing fee on landed cost from the buyer, or a resale spread on consignment goods. Add trustee-side success fees where the desk increases estate recovery. Duties and fees are pre-funded by the buyer, so the desk avoids inventory risk in the early phase.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A container of orphaned goods is worth its inventory value minus the clock. The party that can solve four separate systems (bill-of-lading rights, the carrier lien and demurrage, customs entry and IOR, and compliance screening) in days captures the discount. VCs treat liquidation as a marketplace problem. It is a legal-plumbing problem, and only a customs broker knows how the entry, bond and purchaser-as-IOR pieces fit together.
ideas.first_30_days: Line up a partner bond agent for single-transaction bonds and one buyer network of 5-10 off-price and closeout buyers. Call demurrage collections and terminal-side contacts at 10 carriers and 10 CFS warehouses with a simple offer: we clear abandoned cargo if you waive charges. Ask two bankruptcy trustees whether any estate holds cargo. Close the first 2-3 rescues in the 30-60 day window with fully buyer-funded duties.

ideas.title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
ideas.one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
ideas.customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
ideas.problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
ideas.solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
ideas.why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
ideas.revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.

ideas.title: Blue Tarp Index: Adjuster Ground Truth for ILS
ideas.one_liner: A subscription that sells cat-bond and reinsurance investors what veteran field adjusters can see in the first 10 days after a disaster, before any model or carrier report exists.
ideas.customer: ILS funds, cat bond trading desks, reinsurance-broker analytics teams, and hedge-fund or equity analysts covering Florida, Gulf and California-exposed carriers. Roughly $30k-$120k per year per team.
ideas.problem: Post-event loss estimates swing wildly (Milton was pegged anywhere from a few tens of billions up, and cat-bond implied-loss marks moved daily) and settle slowly. The cat bond market is now about $65.6B outstanding after a record $17.6B of H1 2026 issuance, and most of that capital marks to modeler guesses and carrier press releases. Investors have no structured ground truth for the variables that decide severity: how many roofs really failed, whether demand surge is 10% or 40%, and whether contractors can staff repairs at all.
ideas.solution: A vetted panel of 60-150 independent veteran cat adjusters files 10-minute standardized mobile observations on publicly visible conditions only: blue-tarp density per 100 roofs on sampled blocks, roofing debris and dumpster counts, mystery-shopped contractor and tarp-crew quotes ($/sq, lead times), hotel and RV occupancy, and adjuster deployment density. Outputs are an event dashboard, a 'Blue Tarp Index' and a demand-surge index within 72 hours to 10 days, a weekly note, and paid expert calls. Hard rule, reviewed by counsel: no claim-file, policyholder or carrier-confidential information, only public observation and market pricing, aggregated and anonymized.
ideas.why_now: Cat bond and ILS capital hit records in 2026, with over $120B of ILS capacity, so more money is exposed to event-loss uncertainty than ever. Claims-adjuster employment fell about 21% year over year through May 2026 as carriers automate, which leaves a large pool of experienced people who need income and are cheap to recruit. The very quiet 2026 Atlantic season (no hurricane until at least Sept 11) gives a scrappy team time to build and back-test before the next event. Wildfire, hail and flood events also count as live tests.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual subscription tiers ($25k signal-only, $60k with expert calls, $120k+ bespoke event coverage), per-event pay-per-call expert sessions, and paid retrospective studies. Adjusters get $75-$150 per completed field report plus a revenue share pool. Gross margin is high because the data is field labor, not infrastructure.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Models price wind and exposure, but severity in the real world is set by contractor capacity: how many roofers, tarp crews and drying crews physically exist within 200 miles. An adjuster feels that constraint on day 4 because they cannot get a tarp crew to a house, and nobody in finance measures it. Tarps are also what the policy pays for first, so their density is a fast, visible proxy for claim frequency. The hypothesis is testable by back-testing against Helene, Milton and the LA fires.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 25 laid-off or semi-retired cat adjusters from cat-adjuster Facebook groups, adjuster forums and LinkedIn. Draft the observation protocol and a counsel-approved compliance memo. Run a retrospective 'what we would have told you on day 7' study on Helene/Milton and the Jan 2025 LA fires using panel memory, public imagery and contractor pricing archives. Publish a free sample note, send it to 15 ILS portfolio managers and 5 broker analytics heads, and aim for 2-3 paid pilots ($15-25k) that include the retro study as a deliverable, with the first live test on spring 2027 hail or a wildfire.

ideas.title: Surge Beds: Pre-Contracted Lodging for Catastrophe Responders
ideas.one_liner: Sell adjuster firms and storm contractors reserved-bed options on inland RV pads, seasonal parks and closed motels, contracted before landfall at prices that stay legal after an emergency declaration.
ideas.customer: Independent-adjuster firms' cat operations and logistics managers, restoration franchisees, roofing and mitigation contractors bringing out-of-state crews, and utility subcontractors. Reservation fees are paid pre-season, activation nights after the event.
ideas.problem: After landfall or a big wildfire, responder capacity is limited by beds, not people. Adjusters sleep in cars, 90 minutes away, or in RVs on borrowed lots, and deployed adjusters quit or rotate out. Anti-gouging laws (34 states, typically capping increases at about 10% for 30 days after a declaration) stop hotels from raising rates, so price cannot allocate scarce rooms; they simply sell out to whoever had a relationship or a corporate block.
ideas.solution: A lodging-capacity option network. Sign inland owners 60-150 miles from likely landfall zones (seasonal RV parks and park-model communities that sit empty in hurricane season, church halls and school gyms, closed-for-season motels, dorms, and short-term-rental owners willing to accept 30-day minimum stays) to pre-agreed rates that are lawful because they were set before the emergency. Buyers pay a per-bed or per-site reservation fee before the season, credited against activation nights. Add paid extras that responders actually need: Starlink, laundry, catering, portable showers, secure parking for trucks and trailers. Extend to wildfire base camps in CA, OR and CO.
ideas.why_now: Quick searches surfaced no dedicated adjuster-lodging option marketplace, only ad hoc use of RV parks after storms like Michael. Two years of quiet U.S. hurricane landfalls (none in 2025, and no hurricane at all in the 2026 Atlantic season through Sept 11) mean firms have not tested surge logistics and will be caught out by the next big one. Adjuster and contractor headcounts are being squeezed by automation and tight margins, so a predictable per-bed cost is more attractive than scrambling. Anti-gouging enforcement has grown more aggressive.
ideas.revenue_model: Reservation fees of roughly $400-$900 per bed per season, credited against activation nights. On activation, a 15-20% margin over the pre-agreed owner rate, plus ancillary services (connectivity, meals, laundry) at 30-40% margin. Later, annual enterprise contracts with IA firms for guaranteed headcount blocks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Because gouging laws freeze price after the declaration, the only legal way to buy certainty is to contract early, which turns lodging into an options market where the option seller (a snowbird RV park empty from June to October) has almost no other use for its inventory in exactly the months responders need it. Insiders know the constraint on a cat deployment is where 200 adjusters sleep, not how many exist.
ideas.first_30_days: Call 50 seasonal RV parks, campgrounds and small motel owners across the inland Gulf Coast, Carolinas and Texas and sign non-binding LOIs on rates and bed counts. Draft a one-page option contract reviewed by a hospitality lawyer for gouging-law compliance. Pitch logistics managers at 8 IA firms and restoration franchise groups on 2027 pre-season blocks, aiming for 2-3 signed reservation deposits of 20-50 beds each. Build a simple booking and check-in app with texted access codes and a map of inventory.

ideas.title: Baseline: Bank-Feed Proof of Displacement Costs
ideas.one_liner: An app that reconstructs a displaced family's 'normal' spending from pre-loss bank statements and computes the exact increase that Additional Living Expense coverage owes, in carrier-ready format.
ideas.customer: Public adjusters and disaster-recovery nonprofits (paying per file), and carriers or TPAs handling long-tail displaced-household claims (paying per active ALE file per month). Consumers use it free.
ideas.problem: ALE pays the increase over normal living costs, not the total, so proving it requires a baseline that almost no family has. Adjusters spend hours rebuilding it from memory and shoeboxes, families under-claim (groceries, laundry, mileage, pet boarding, storage, higher utilities) or document sloppily, and disputes turn ugly. With California's new smoke-damage law (AB 1795, effective Jan 1, 2027) barring insurers from cutting off ALE until the home is restored, thousands of standing-home households will run ALE claims for years with heavy documentation demands.
ideas.solution: A privacy-first tool that ingests 12 months of pre-loss bank or card data (via open-banking link or uploaded statements), builds a per-category baseline, then diffs it month by month against post-loss spending, matches receipts, and flags gaps the family can legitimately claim (extra mileage, meal delta, rented furniture, storage). Output is an ALE ledger with audit trail in the format desk adjusters actually accept, plus a deadline tracker for policy ALE time limits. Processing is on-device or in a private enclave, and the data is deleted after export.
ideas.why_now: More than 13,000 standing-home smoke claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires are still unresolved 20 months later, a lawsuit accuses Farmers' vendor of substandard assessments, and AB 1795 makes ALE duration a live issue. LLM parsing of messy statements and receipts is now cheap and accurate enough to be a product. Carriers are cutting adjusters (entry-level postings down about 50% since 2025) but ALE files still need documentation, so automation that delivers clean files is welcomed.
ideas.revenue_model: Public adjusters and recovery groups pay $99-$199 per file. Carriers and TPAs pay $30-$60 per active ALE file per month, or $75-$150 per closed file, in exchange for fewer touches and fewer complaints. Optional referral fees from moving, storage and rental-furniture vendors for legitimate, claimable purchases.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the industry records 'normal.' The claim's central number, the increase over normal, is unmeasured on the policyholder's side, and adjusters know most under-claiming is not a coverage denial but the family's inability to prove what they used to spend. Bank data is the only pre-loss record the insured always has.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a prototype that categorizes statement CSVs and PDFs into ALE categories and produces a monthly delta ledger. Offer it free to 10 Altadena and Palisades public adjusters and to two survivor-support networks in exchange for feedback and 20 anonymized-consent pilot files. Ask two carrier ALE desk managers to review the output format and sign a paid pilot at $50 per file for 200 files. Prepare a privacy policy and data-deletion promise, because trust is the product.

ideas.title: Loss Draft Desk for Storm Contractors
ideas.one_liner: Software and concierge service that gets contractors and homeowners through the mortgage servicer's loss-draft process, then advances cash against approved draws.
ideas.customer: Storm-restoration general contractors, roofers and owner-builders working on mortgage-encumbered repairs and rebuilds, starting with the Palisades and Eaton rebuild wave and Gulf Coast stragglers. Later, homeowners and the servicers' own vendor teams.
ideas.problem: The carrier pays, but the money is not free: the check names the mortgagee, and the servicer's loss-draft department decides whether to release it in one lump sum or in staged draws tied to inspections. Each servicer has its own packet (contractor W-9, license, signed contract, lien waivers, before/after photos, inspection scheduling) and its own cadence. Contractors carry 60-120 days of working capital risk, homeowners cannot start work, and adjusters take the blame for a delay that comes after the estimate is done.
ideas.solution: A draw-management platform: it reads the carrier's payment letter and the servicer's requirements, auto-builds and submits the servicer-specific packet, schedules and preps for inspections (checklist plus timestamped photo capture), chases the servicer, and shows the contractor and homeowner a live 'money timeline.' Phase two adds a draw advance: after the servicer approves a draw schedule, the platform advances 80-90% of the next draw in days, underwritten on proprietary servicer-by-servicer release data.
ideas.why_now: Florida's AOB ban (for policies since 2023) means contractors cannot be paid directly by carriers, so they must wait on homeowners and servicers. The LA fire rebuild in 2026-27 involves thousands of large, mortgage-encumbered claims and long draw schedules. Materials costs remain volatile, which squeezes contractor cash. Regulatory rules and GSE guidelines push servicers to release funds promptly after approving a repair plan but leave the mechanics unstandardized, creating a compliance-flavored process that software can systematize.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat $295-$495 per job, or 0.5-1% of funds released. Draw advances at 2-3% of advance amount plus a 30-60 day fee, funded by a warehouse credit line. Later, per-file fees from servicers who want clean packets and fewer complaint escalations.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real payment terms in disaster repair are the servicer's draw curve, not the insurance company's payment speed, and nobody publishes it. Whoever logs, servicer by servicer, days-to-first-draw, inspection pass rates and packet rejection reasons owns the underwriting data for the only safe lending against insurance proceeds.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign up 5 mid-size LA fire rebuild contractors and 5 Gulf Coast roofers and offer to run their next 3 jobs through the loss-draft process as a done-for-you service at $295 per job. Log every servicer requirement in a shared spreadsheet, then turn it into a rules engine. Interview 3 former loss-draft department employees for packet-rejection patterns. Start collecting draw-timeline data, which becomes the moat and the basis for a later advance product.

ideas.title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
ideas.one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
ideas.customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
ideas.problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
ideas.solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
ideas.why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.

ideas.title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
ideas.one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
ideas.customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
ideas.problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
ideas.solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
ideas.why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.

ideas.title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
ideas.one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
ideas.customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
ideas.problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
ideas.solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
ideas.why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.

ideas.title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
ideas.one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
ideas.customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
ideas.problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
ideas.solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
ideas.why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.

ideas.title: Payer Offset and Recoupment Radar
ideas.one_liner: Reconstruct the silent payer clawbacks buried in the 835 provider-level adjustment segment, then dispute the ones that lack notice or exceed state look-back limits.
ideas.customer: Community and mid-size hospitals, physician groups and MSOs, and RCM outsourcers who want a recovery line item. SaaS at $1-3k/month, or 15-25% of reversed recoupments.
ideas.problem: Payers increasingly claw money back by netting it inside the electronic remittance (835) PLB provider-level balance segment, or by short-paying unrelated claims. These adjustments carry cryptic reason codes and no patient or claim detail. Cash posters drop them into a suspense or 'other adjustment' account, or write them off. The overpayment letters that justify them arrive by mail, fax or random emails and are never matched. Many states cap retroactive recoupment look-back windows and require claim-level notice, but no one checks whether the payer complied.
ideas.solution: Ingest 12-24 months of 835s and the payer's overpayment and audit letters (PDF/email/fax OCR). Rebuild every offset to claim level. Flag recoupments with no valid notice, past the state or contract look-back, duplicating a prior recoupment, or hitting claims already appealed. Generate dispute letters and track outcomes. A payer scorecard shows clawback dollars per $1M paid, which gives the CFO leverage at contract renewal.
ideas.why_now: Payer payment-integrity programs are scaling with AI-driven post-payment audits and coding-policy downcodes. Medicare Advantage audit pressure is rising. Hospitals staffed thin after the 2025-26 Medicaid and margin squeeze cannot chase each offset by hand. Post-payment recoupment is the fastest-growing part of the denial problem and the least instrumented.
ideas.revenue_model: Contingency 15-25% of recoupments reversed, or $1-3k/month per facility for monitoring plus a $5-10k onboarding audit. Payer scorecards can be sold to hospital associations.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Denial management tools watch denied claims. Recoupments are not denied claims. They are negative dollars in the remit file that nobody owns. Only cash posters see them and they are told to just post them. In a typical mid-size hospital these unmatched offsets total mid-six to seven figures a year, and dispute success is highest exactly where the payer skipped required notice. The data is already sitting in files the hospital owns.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask 5 friendly hospital and group cash-posting managers for 12 months of 835s (clearinghouses can export them), which requires only a BAA. Write a parser for the PLB segments (about a week of work) and produce a 'recoupment leakage report' showing unmatched offset dollars per payer. Use the number to sign 2 contingency pilots, and build the letter-matching module on real customer data.

ideas.title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
ideas.one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
ideas.customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
ideas.problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
ideas.solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
ideas.why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

ideas.title: Real-Pixel Blink Fixer for Family Formals
ideas.one_liner: A Lightroom/Photoshop plugin that turns a 5-frame burst of the 30-person family formal into one frame where every set of eyes is open, using only real pixels from the burst and no generated faces.
ideas.customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers (roughly 100k in the US), paying $29-49/mo or about $2 per composite. Later extension: school, team, church and corporate group-portrait photographers.
ideas.problem: Family formals are the 20-40 minute block of the day that grandparents care about most. They are also mathematically hostile. If each person has their eyes closed about 8% of the time, a 30-person frame has under a 10% chance of everyone being open, before counting people who look away or squint. So the delivered frame is nearly always a compromise or a composite. Photographers either hand-swap heads in Photoshop (20-40 minutes per group, or $15-40 per image if outsourced), ship the frame with the blinker, or use generative fill. Generative fill invents a face, which is a betrayal when the face is a grandfather who won't be there in two years.
ideas.solution: Drop in the formals folder. The tool groups frames into bursts, aligns them (people shift between frames), scores each person's face for eyes open, smile, gaze and sharpness, picks the best patch per person, and blends with seam-aware masks. The output is a layered PSD so the photographer can override any face in one click. The pitch is a strict 'zero generative pixels' guarantee. A second mode is a shoot-time phone companion that says 'frame 3 has 2 blinkers, shoot one more' so bursts are captured with enough variety. The wedge is batch mode for formals only, not a full editor.
ideas.why_now: Google's Best Take (Pixel 8, 2023) taught consumers to expect a merged best-expression group photo. Photographers already pay monthly for AI culling and editing, so AI tooling is normal spend in this trade. Adobe's own face-swap route leans on generative fill, which many pros distrust for client faces. On-device face-landmark and eye-state models are now cheap and accurate enough to run locally on a laptop. Searches in Sept 2026 found only manual Photoshop tutorials for this, not a dedicated automated burst-composite product.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription of $29/mo for solo shooters or $2 per composite credit with monthly bundles. Studio plans at $79/mo. Optional white-label API for gallery platforms (Pic-Time, ShootProof-type) later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody outside the trade realizes that a truly 'perfect' 30-person frame almost never exists in a single exposure, so every delivered formal is quietly a fix or a compromise. The fix that matters is provenance: the people who print the formals at 16x20 are the elderly relatives, and they will notice an AI-invented face on Grandpa. 'Real pixels only' is the actual feature, not the face-swapping.
ideas.first_30_days: Build against Lightroom Classic/Photoshop with open-source face-landmark models. Ask 20 photographers in Facebook groups and r/WeddingPhotography to send 3 old formals bursts from past weddings (every working shooter has hundreds sitting in archives). Return composites in 24 hours with before/after slider pages. First 10 composites free, then $2 each via Stripe. Post the before/afters and blink-probability math in photographer communities. Goal is 30 paying studios and one gallery-platform partnership conversation by day 90.

ideas.title: Mailed Proof Books for Grandparents Who Buy Prints
ideas.one_liner: Turn a wedding gallery into a personalized printed booklet, mailed to each grandparent and parent with a phone number to order prints, because the people who actually pay for wedding prints never click gallery links.
ideas.customer: Wedding photographers (they pay only via revenue share). The end payers are the couple's parents, in-laws and grandparents, who spend $150-400 per household on prints and albums.
ideas.problem: The dirty secret of studio economics is that couples buy almost nothing after delivery. They have the gallery and Instagram. The people who buy prints and albums are mothers, mothers-in-law and grandparents, and the photographer's only delivery channel is a link emailed to the couple, who rarely forward it. Pic-Time and similar platforms added face-recognition and selfie-search galleries in late 2025, but that assumes a phone-comfortable guest willing to scan their face on a website. Grandma will not do that. Every wedding leaves an estimated $500-2,000 of print revenue uncollected, and the 'last photo with Grandpa' has a clock on it.
ideas.solution: The photographer uploads the gallery and the family list (they already have it from the formals shot list). We cluster faces, have the photographer confirm the 6-12 key elders and parents, and auto-build a 16-24 page softcover booklet per person ('Nana's Book: 22 photos of you and your grandkids'). We print and mail it within about 10 days of gallery delivery, with the couple's opt-in and a handwritten-style note from them. Every booklet carries a QR code plus a toll-free number answered first by a human and later by a voice agent that takes orders by phone and card, with check-by-mail as an option. Orders are fulfilled through pro labs, and the photographer sees a dashboard of sales.
ideas.why_now: AI face search has just become standard in photographer gallery platforms (Pic-Time's Nov 2025 update), which proves photographers will pay for AI galleries but leaves the elder channel unserved. Softcover print-on-demand now lands at roughly $6-10 for a 24-page book via lab and POD APIs. 2026-grade voice agents can take a print order from a 78-year-old who hates websites. Wedding-guest demographics are also aging, since couples are marrying later and grandparents are still at the table.
ideas.revenue_model: No upfront fee to the photographer. We front the booklet cost (about $10 landed) and keep roughly 40% of resulting print and album order revenue at lab retail, with the photographer keeping 60%, which is pure incremental margin. Optional $15 flat per-booklet pricing for photographers who want to buy outright.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the client. The couple's inbox is the wrong channel, and a personalized object with the recipient's own face on it is something people do not throw away. The product is a channel to 60-85-year-olds who respond to paper and phone calls, and the gallery software is just the data source.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 photographers from local and online groups who delivered a wedding in the last 6 months. Produce booklets for 2 of their weddings each, at your cost (about $100 in print and postage per wedding), using a Pic-Time/ShootProof export, open-source face clustering (InsightFace) and a lab or Lulu/Blurb-style API. Route the phone number to the founder's cell. Track orders per booklet. If 1 in 5 booklets converts to a $100+ order, sign the rev-share terms and scale to 50 studios.

ideas.title: Reserve-Crew Backup Photographers for Wedding Day Emergencies
ideas.one_liner: A paid-standby bench of pre-vetted, style-matched backup photographers who can be dispatched within 2-3 hours, sold to solo photographers as a subscription and to wedding insurers as claims fulfillment.
ideas.customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers ($199-399/yr for a 'Continuity Guarantee' they can promise couples), plus wedding-insurance carriers and MGAs that cover vendor failure but cannot produce a person.
ideas.problem: Every solo photographer's nightmare is a sudden illness, crash or family emergency six hours before a wedding. The standard backup plan in contracts is 'a photographer friend', which fails in practice. On peak Saturdays (dates like 10/10/26) every competent local shooter is already booked, so the Facebook SOS post at 6am gets 40 sympathetic comments and zero style-matched, available humans. Whoever does show up has never seen the timeline, venue notes, family-formals list or the photographer's look. Wedding insurance reimburses money after the fact but cannot supply a competent human in three hours. It is a capacity-reservation problem, not an insurance problem.
ideas.solution: Members upload style samples plus a 'Continuity Pack' for each booked wedding (timeline, family list, venue and light notes, gallery drop link), all in one place. We maintain a regional bench of vetted shooters tagged by style (documentary, bright and airy, moody, film-look). Bench shooters are paid a small standby retainer (about $40) to hold peak dates, plus an activation fee ($500-900) paid by the member or the insurer. On activation, the pack is pushed to the understudy, a coordinator handles couple communication, and images are delivered under the member's brand. Members display a 'Continuity Guaranteed' badge, which becomes a booking-conversion asset.
ideas.why_now: Vendor-failure cover is now a standard add-on in wedding insurance, and 2026 contracts increasingly require a comparable replacement or a full refund, so the gap between reimbursing money and supplying a photographer is now visible and contractual. Weekend supply is squeezed onto peak dates, and a growing pool of freelance portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open weekends can be organized cheaply through Stripe Connect and shared workspaces. Insurers are also under pressure to reduce claim severity in small commercial lines.
ideas.revenue_model: $99-399/yr member subscription (tiered by number of weddings), per-activation fee split with the bench shooter (we keep about 20%), and an insurer contract of a flat per-policy fee or per-claim fulfillment fee. Standby retainers are funded from the subscription pool, like airline reserve crews.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Backup fails precisely on the dates it is needed, because scarcity is correlated. The free 'photographer friend' network evaporates on peak Saturdays. The only fix is paying for reserved capacity in advance, and once you do, you own the only reliable answer to the industry's most feared event.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign 25 solo photographers as founding members at $99/yr and recruit 8 bench shooters (portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open Saturdays). Build the Continuity Pack in Notion/Airtable plus a shared Google Drive. Run a fire drill: on a chosen Saturday, ping every member's pack and time how fast each is delivered to a bench shooter. Pitch two wedding-insurance MGAs on a 90-day claims-fulfillment pilot, and get a lawyer to check contractor and liability terms before the first live activation.

ideas.title: Verified-Real Dating Portraits Shot by Wedding Photographers
ideas.one_liner: A consumer brand that rents wedding photographers' dead winter months to shoot candid-directed dating and profile portraits, delivered with a signed 'real photo' certificate.
ideas.customer: Single adults aged 25-45 in the top 20 US metros paying $179-299 per session. Secondary channel: matchmakers and dating coaches buying sessions for their clients.
ideas.problem: Wedding photographers earn most of their income in a compressed May-October window and sit mostly idle from November to March, with skills and gear already paid for. Meanwhile dating profiles are flooded with AI-generated and heavily retouched photos, so users and matches increasingly distrust every photo. Existing options are cheap AI headshot apps (the very thing everyone distrusts), generic corporate headshot studios that make stiff LinkedIn photos, and a few dating-photo studios with model-y aesthetics. Nobody is selling authenticity as a verifiable, human-shot product.
ideas.solution: A productized 60-minute walk-and-talk shoot across three locations using wedding-style directing prompts ('walk toward me and tell me the worst first date you've had') that get natural laughter from stiff people in about 90 seconds. Delivery is 15 edited photos in 48 hours following a dating shot list (full-body, hobby, social proof, pet, non-selfie smile). Each set ships with a 'Real Photo Certificate': Content Credentials (C2PA) from supported cameras, a no-generative-AI editing policy, and a public verification page users can link in their bio. Supply comes from wedding photographers trained in a 90-minute module. The platform handles booking, payment, brand, marketing and QC and keeps 30-35%.
ideas.why_now: AI-generated profile photos are now common enough that dating apps have leaned on photo and face verification. Several major camera makers now ship Content Credentials support in newer bodies or firmware, so provenance is technically feasible for small studios. Wedding photographers are also under margin pressure as couples trim coverage hours and guest counts, so winter income is increasingly attractive. 2026 is the first year 'proof a human made this' has real consumer value.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-299 per session with a 30-35% platform take. Upsells include a $39 'profile audit' and a re-shoot at 6 months. B2B2C packages for matchmakers and dating coaches at $150 per client.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce skill isn't lighting, it's getting a stiff stranger to laugh convincingly on cue, which wedding photographers do 40 times a summer. The photographer's marginal cost in January is close to zero, so supply arrives almost free while every competitor pays full-time studio rents.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro and recruit 6 wedding photographers who complain publicly about winter. Run 20 pilot shoots at a $99 launch price, sourced from local Instagram/Reddit dating communities, run clubs and singles events, and from 5 matchmakers and dating coaches. Ask each client for before/after match counts (self-reported) and permission to publish testimonials. Register a public verification page for each set. Charge full price from shoot 21 onward.

ideas.title: Ritual-Accurate Wedding Data and Audits for AI
ideas.one_liner: Commission consented, styled ceremony shoots with community elders across a dozen wedding traditions, captioned by ritual stage, and sell accuracy audits and licensed datasets to image-model builders and wedding-tech companies.
ideas.customer: Generative-image model builders, stock and creative platforms with AI-licensing programs, and wedding-tech companies building AI mood boards or visualizers. Audits are $5-15k each and dataset packs are $20-150k.
ideas.problem: Image generators still get weddings wrong outside the mainstream Western template, and research on cultural bias in image models documents mis-styled Indian weddings, misidentified Korean attire and mislocalized Nigerian scenes. Web-scraped labels are worse, since 'Indian wedding' collapses Sikh, Tamil, Gujarati and Bengali ceremonies. Couples now bring AI 'inspiration' images to photographers, and wedding-tech startups embarrass themselves with visualizers that get rituals wrong in the multi-day, high-budget segments they most want. The scarce resource isn't wedding pictures, it's correctly labeled, ritual-stage-accurate images with clean releases.
ideas.solution: Rite Right runs one- and two-day ritual shoots with paid models, real officiants and community elders as advisors (no unconsented guests, so licensing is clean), photographed by working wedding pros in documentary style.
