Each image gets structured metadata: tradition, region, ritual stage, garment and object names, and a community-authored accuracy checklist, with model and property releases and C2PA provenance. Product one is the audit, a 'Wedding Ritual Accuracy Benchmark' (about 50 prompts per tradition) scored by elders on public and private models. Product two is licensed packs. Photographers and advisors share in license revenue.
ideas.why_now: AI-training licensing has become a real market, since Adobe and Shutterstock run contributor payout programs for training use and Getty has an OpenAI deal. Lawsuits are pushing labs toward clean, consented data, and cultural-bias evaluation of image models is an active research area. AI wedding visualizers are proliferating, and their cultural errors are viral, embarrassing and commercially costly. Audits are cheap, fast and require no dataset, so they provide first revenue while the data business builds.
ideas.revenue_model: Accuracy audits at $5-15k each (repeat quarterly as models update), dataset licensing at $20-150k per tradition pack, and rev-share to photographers and advisors. Later: a 'ritual accuracy' API for wedding-tech products.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The photographer who has shot 40 Sikh weddings can tell in three seconds whether a laavan sequence is wrong, and that knowledge is oral, undocumented and invisible to crowd-worker labeling. What data buyers lack is not volume but the moment-by-moment ritual sequence, and only people who stand in the room at these events can supply it credibly.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 community advisors across 3 traditions from your own network. Run one styled one-day shoot on a $4-6k budget and build a 300-image sample pack with structured captions. Build a 50-prompt accuracy benchmark, score the major public image models, and publish the results as a short report to generate inbound. Email trust and safety, data and product leads at mid-size model builders and wedding-tech companies with the report and a free 10-image sample, aiming for two paid pilot audits by day 90.

ideas.title: Evacuation Lift Registry Ending Double-Booked Buses
ideas.one_liner: A neutral county-level registry that guarantees each ambulance, wheelchair van and bus seat is promised to only one nursing home per storm, paid for by facilities and by carriers who finally get standby retainers.
ideas.customer: Paying: multi-site nursing home and assisted-living operators (SaaS per facility) and ambulance/NEMT/charter-bus operators (platform fee on standby retainers). Sponsoring: county emergency managers and healthcare coalitions using preparedness grants.
ideas.problem: The CMS emergency preparedness rule makes every facility hold transportation agreements, but no one checks whether the same 40 wheelchair vans and ambulances are 'contracted' by 300 facilities. GAO and post-Katrina research found carriers holding contracts with many facilities in one community, which works for a single-building evacuation and collapses when a whole county goes at once. Facilities learn at H-48 that their contract is one of a dozen identical promises. Carriers do not honor a promise they were never paid to hold.
ideas.solution: Borrow the military's lift-allocation discipline, where an asset can appear on the movement plan only once. Facilities reserve capacity by resident mix (ambulatory, wheelchair, stretcher, oxygen or vent-dependent), not by 'beds'. The registry totals promised demand against real vehicle capacity by county and flags oversubscription weeks before the season, then matches the gap to out-of-region carriers on paid standby. At activation it issues a departure-window movement table so convoys do not collide, plus manifest and accountability packets for each facility. Before activation it stores only aggregate counts by acuity, not PHI, which keeps HIPAA scope small.
ideas.why_now: The President's FEMA Review Council final report (May 7, 2026) recommends disaster response be 'locally executed, state managed, federally supported'. Counties and healthcare coalitions are inheriting logistics they never staffed, with less federal backfill. It is peak hurricane season, and post-acute care closures and consolidation are concentrating residents into fewer, larger buildings.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per facility per month. Carriers pay 8-12% on standby retainers the platform brokers, which they never received before. Optional county or coalition license of $25-100k a year, funded by ASPR HPP or EMPG grants. Later, add-ons for dialysis centers, group homes and inpatient rehab.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Vehicles are not the shortage. Unique promises are. Every evacuation failure post-mortem says 'not enough buses', but the fleet often exists and is simply committed many times over. Military movement planners never let one lift asset appear twice on a time-phased deployment plan, while civilian planners have nobody whose job is to check. Loading time is also the hidden constraint: a stretcher resident takes about 20 minutes to load, so acuity mix, not headcount, determines how many vehicles you need.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one storm-prone county cluster (Tampa Bay, coastal Carolinas or Louisiana parishes). Ask 10 facilities to share their transport MOUs, which they must keep on file for CMS surveys anyway. Build the overlap heat map by hand in a spreadsheet, for example 'nine of your ten facilities are promised the same carrier'. Take it to the county emergency manager and the healthcare coalition coordinator. Convert 3-5 facilities to a paid pilot at about $200 a month and sign 2 carriers to retainer contracts. Build the product as Airtable plus a simple web form before writing real software.

ideas.title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
ideas.one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
ideas.customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
ideas.problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
ideas.solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
ideas.why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.

ideas.title: Pre-Surveyed Superload Corridors for Data Center Freight
ideas.one_liner: A subscription library of continuously re-verified main supply routes for 100-400 ton transformer and switchgear moves, so heavy-haul carriers stop paying for a bespoke route survey on the same corridors every time.
ideas.customer: Heavy-haul carriers and project-cargo forwarders moving transformers, switchgear and generators to data centers and substations. Secondary buyers are EPC contractors, equipment OEMs and state permit offices.
ideas.problem: Every superload needs a route survey covering bridge ratings, turn radii, overhead lines, signals, rail crossings and escort rules. It costs weeks and real money, and it is repeated from scratch for the same handful of corridors from ports and rail heads to the same data-center clusters. Transformer deliveries are project cargo booked years ahead, and the domestic flatbed leg is at its tightest in years. The delay that kills schedules is rarely the bridge. It is the utility that needs six weeks and a bucket-truck crew to lift a line.
ideas.solution: Treat major corridors like military main supply routes: classify them once, then re-verify on a cycle. A survey crew captures mobile LiDAR, 360 imagery and pole-height data on a fixed corridor, then builds a route package with go/no-go strip maps and choke-point drawings. Each choke point carries the owner and the lead time to clear it (which utility, how many weeks, what it costs, which county road closures and escort rules apply). Sell annual corridor subscriptions, with an engineer-stamped per-move certification as an add-on. Recruit surveyors from retired combat engineers and route-reconnaissance veterans.
ideas.why_now: Data-center buildout is turning transformers into the pacing item. Industry reporting expects annual U.S. transformer demand to rise from roughly 1,500 units today toward 9,000 by 2030, with about 12 GW of capacity announced across roughly 140 projects for 2026 but only about 5 GW under construction. Forwarders now lock in manufacturing slots, ports and heavy-haul routes years ahead, and the trucking leg has a second lead-time problem.
ideas.revenue_model: Corridor subscription of about $15-60k a year per carrier per corridor, per-move engineer-certified route stamp of $3-10k, and data licenses to OEMs, developers and forwarders who want pre-clearance before quoting a delivery date.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Route knowledge decays, and reuse is high. A few dozen corridors carry most loads, so a maintained library beats one-off surveys the way a pre-classified main supply route beats a fresh reconnaissance. The value is freshness (last verified date) and the choke-point ownership map, not the imagery. Carriers will trade permission to reuse survey data for a discount on their own move, which funds the first corridors.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose one corridor with a live job, such as a Gulf Coast port to a Texas data-center cluster or a feeder route into a Northern Virginia campus. Offer a friendly heavy-haul carrier a discounted survey of its actual move in exchange for the right to reuse the data. Use a rented or $30-40k rig (GNSS, laser pole, 360 camera) and 2 veterans with route-reconnaissance or heavy-haul permit experience. Package the deliverable, then sell corridor #2 to that carrier's competitors and to a transformer OEM's logistics manager.

ideas.title: Serial-Level Collateral Registry for GPU Lenders
ideas.one_liner: The independent field-exam firm and cross-lender double-pledge registry for AI hardware debt, built on the military rule that a serial number appears on one hand receipt only.
ideas.customer: Private-credit funds, banks, equipment lessors, ABS trustees and insurers financing neocloud GPU fleets, which now hold well over $20 billion in GPU-backed debt. Secondary: neoclouds that need audit-ready proof to borrow at lower spreads.
ideas.problem: Lenders rely on borrower-supplied serial lists, telemetry and occasional inspections. After the Tricolor and First Brands double-pledging scandals (the SEC charged Tricolor's former executives in August 2026), lenders know 'the same collateral pledged twice' is real. GPU servers sit in multi-tenant colocation halls, are easy to move, swap or re-pledge to another SPV, and telemetry can be spoofed. Serial-number UCC filings are rarely searched across lenders, and a colo technician paid by the borrower is not an independent counter.
ideas.solution: Three layers. (1) A repeatable two-person independent inventory protocol: witnessed reads of chassis label, BMC out-of-band serial and GPU-level serial, plus rack and cage photos, location and power draw. (2) Serialized tamper-evident seals on cages and rack doors, checked at each visit. (3) A privacy-preserving cross-lender registry of hashed serials so a lender learns whether a serial is already pledged elsewhere without revealing its book. Deliver monthly compliance packages that plug into the loan's reporting covenants for the trustee.
ideas.why_now: GPU-backed lending crossed $20 billion, and CoreWeave's $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan (March 2026) showed the asset class reaching investment-grade structures. Tricolor and First Brands made 'verify the collateral independently' a board-level demand in private credit. Loan documents already grant lenders inspection rights, so the buyer has the access but not the in-house field-exam capability. Export-control diversion risk adds a second reason for chain-of-custody evidence.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-site audit of $15-50k, annual monitoring retainer of $50-250k per facility, registry subscriptions of $50-200k per lender, and trustee or insurer reporting packages. Long-term, per-basis-point fees on financed collateral under verification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives at the seam between paper and physical, and the only reliable control is a count by someone who does not report to the borrower. That is what a military property book officer and a sensitive-item inventory do. Lenders will not share collateral lists with each other but will share hashes to avoid being second in line, so the registry becomes the moat. Telemetry proves a box is powered on, not that it is the box you financed.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 former property book or supply officers plus a data-center operations technician. Write and publish the audit protocol. Approach 5 mid-tier credit funds and equipment lenders (not the giants) that do GPU deals and lack field-exam staff. Offer a fixed-fee pilot audit on a live deal using the lender's existing inspection rights. Get a securities and privacy lawyer to bless the hashed-serial registry design before any lender data is pooled.

ideas.title: Government Property Control Kit for New Defense Makers
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price property-system-in-a-box (tags, procedures, mock audit, reconciliation) that keeps first-time defense manufacturers from failing their government property audit and having payments withheld.
ideas.customer: New-entrant defense manufacturers (drone, munitions second-source and component startups) and small machine shops that receive government-furnished property, plus primes that flow the property clauses down and want their subs certified.
ideas.problem: Contractors holding government-furnished property must run a property management system with receiving reports, physical inventory, loss and damage reporting, and reconciliation to the contract's property list. If the government disapproves the system, contracting officers can direct payment withholds. Small shops run this on spreadsheets and no one is the accountable hand-receipt holder. Property administrators cannot coach, and consultants bill $200-400 an hour.
ideas.solution: A packaged offering. A one-day on-site 'mock property system analysis' run by former property administrators. Asset tagging and mobile scanning. Templated procedures, forms and a monthly reconciliation to the contract property list. Audit-ready binder and annual physical inventory support. Ongoing loss/damage/destruction reporting and excess-property disposition paperwork. Position it to program managers, not compliance officers, as schedule protection.
ideas.why_now: The Revolutionary FAR Overhaul rewrote Part 45 (Government Property), with model deviation text implemented from November 2025, so many contractors are rereading their obligations. Defense spending and drone and munitions ramp-ups are pulling venture-backed hardware companies and first-time subs into contracts with government-furnished property. CMMC phase-ins compete for the same small compliance budgets, so property control gets ignored until an audit finds it.
ideas.revenue_model: Mock audit at $6-15k, then $500-2,000 a month for software plus fractional property-officer support, plus per-asset tagging fees. Prime-sponsored programs where a prime pays to certify its sub base.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The property system is about 90% behavior and 10% software: who signs for what, and whether there is an unbroken trail from receipt to disposition. Auditors find the same handful of deficiencies again and again (no receiving report, no physical inventory, no reconciliation, no loss report), so a checklist-driven fixed-price service works better than custom consulting. The strongest sponsor is the prime, because a sub's disapproved system threatens the prime's own schedule and cash.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull first-time awardees from SBIR/STTR winners and public contract awards that carry government-furnished property. Offer 10 of them a $2,500 one-day GFP health check. Publish a one-page 'seven findings auditors keep writing' as lead magnet. Partner with a regional APEX Accelerator for referrals and a CMMC registered provider organization for cross-sell. Turn the first 3 engagements into a templated binder and a simple scanning workflow before building any software.

ideas.title: Rescue Orphaned Steno Notes With Stroke-Level AI
ideas.one_liner: A translation service that turns retired or deceased reporters' unreadable steno files into certifiable transcripts for stalled appeals, using a neural stroke-to-text model in place of the missing personal dictionary.
ideas.customer: County and state court administrators, public defender and appellate defender offices, and state AG appellate divisions. Secondary customers are retiring reporters and their estates. The first buyer is an appellate defender office with transcript orders stuck because the reporter left, paying about $2.50-$4 per page with a $1,500 minimum.
ideas.problem: Steno notes are a personal code, not a shared language. Another reporter cannot read them without the writer's dictionary, which holds phonetic strokes plus thousands of private shortcuts called briefs. When a reporter retires, dies or moves away, their untranscribed notes are effectively dead. Appeals stall for months, and courts may have to redo hearings or accept an inadequate record. Retention rules (California is 10 years for criminal cases and 5 for most others) mean old notes are also being boxed up or destroyed as reporters retire. The average reporter is in their mid-50s, and the workforce has shrunk about 21% in a decade.
ideas.solution: Train a stroke-sequence model. Input is the raw stroke stream with timestamps. Output is English with punctuation and Q/A structure. Training data comes from open steno corpora and community theory dictionaries, synthetic strokes with randomized personal-brief variation, and consented archives from retired reporters. Where the reporter also ran a backup audio recording, fuse audio and strokes to resolve homophones. Sell three products. (1) Rescue: per-page conversion, human-scoped by a retired reporter who certifies the transcript as prepared from the original reporter's notes. (2) Archive escrow: retiring reporters pay a one-time fee or a small monthly fee to have notes and dictionary converted, indexed and held by a custodian that satisfies retention rules. (3) Later, a scoping copilot for active reporters, who spend 1-3 hours editing per hour of testimony.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 retirement wave is here, and NCRA-cited data puts the average member age around 56. The 5-10 year retention windows for notes written in 2016-2021 are closing now. California's 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) requires courts to give indigent litigants a verbatim record on request, which will create more appeals that need transcripts. Sequence models can now handle noisy phonetic-to-text conversion with context, and the open steno community (Plover) has published theory and dictionaries.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-page rescue fees, priced below the $4-6 ordinary transcript rate and paid by courts or appellate offices. Escrow and conversion packages for retirees (about $300-$800 one-time, or $25 per month). Annual contracts with court systems for backlog clearing. Later, a $99-$149 per month scoping copilot for active reporters, who already pay $3,000+ for CAT software.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Only the writer can read steno notes. Court administrators do not track how many untranscribed notes sit with reporters about to retire. The stroke stream is also a cleaner input than audio, because a trained human already resolved the speaker, punctuation and homophones in real time. Almost nobody outside the profession knows the raw-notes problem exists.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 retired reporters through state association retiree lists. They donate or license old practice files and act as reviewers and certifiers. Build a baseline model on synthetic and open steno data, then test it blind on their files and record the accuracy. Cold-call 10 appellate defender and public defender offices with one question: do you have appeals stalled because the reporter is unavailable? Close 2-3 paid pilots at the $1,500 minimum.

ideas.title: Sworn Testator Depositions for the Deepfake Era
ideas.one_liner: Estate attorneys refer aging or blended-family clients to a 45-minute sworn Q&A on intent and capacity, taken by a reporter who certifies it and stored in an escrow vault that opens on death. Because a human certified it, it stays credible when video can be faked.
ideas.customer: Estate planning and elder law attorneys, whose clients pay $1,200-$3,000 per session (billed through as a cost). Also wealth advisors and family offices serving blended-family, dementia-risk or high-conflict heirs. Trust and estate litigators are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: The great wealth transfer is driving more will and trust contests over capacity and undue influence. The standard defense is a video of the signing, but anyone can now claim video or audio is synthetic or edited. Attorney file notes look self-serving, and witness memory fades over the 5-15 years between signing and death. Court reporters are the one neutral officer who can administer an oath and certify a verbatim record. Only litigation agencies dispatch reporters, so estate lawyers never think to hire one.
ideas.solution: A productized package. A licensed reporter administers the oath. The attorney or an independent examiner runs a structured interview covering assets, family, reasons for unequal splits, and awareness of who might object. An optional treating-physician attestation is added. The client receives a certified transcript, hash-locked and time-stamped video, and the reporter's certificate. Everything goes into an encrypted escrow vault that releases on a death certificate or an attorney trigger. Clients re-sit every 2-3 years. The package maps to ante-mortem probate options in the few states that have them (Ohio and Alaska are examples) and to each state's rules for perpetuating testimony. Admissibility varies by jurisdiction, so attorneys own the legal strategy.
ideas.why_now: Deepfakes are making courts wary of unauthenticated audio and video. The federal Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules was still working on a Rule 901(c) deepfake amendment and a new Rule 707 for machine-generated evidence at its October 2026 meeting. Remote depositions and remote-reporting laws such as California's AB 3013 make flexible scheduling normal, and estate sessions can be scheduled unlike litigation work. The wealth transfer is under way now.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,200-$3,000 per session, with about 50-60% going to the reporter. Vault fee of about $150 per year. $600 re-sit sessions every 2-3 years, which creates a recurring long tail. No referral fees to attorneys, because ethics rules prohibit fee splitting. Attorneys bill the session as a case cost.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The reporter's certificate and oath are the one part of a transcript AI cannot counterfeit, and its value rises as media authenticity falls. Estate planners sit outside the reporter dispatch network, so nobody has packaged the reporter's authority for them.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2 licensed reporters and 1 estate attorney, ideally in a large metro or an ante-mortem-probate state. Write the interview protocol with the attorney and a geriatric psychiatrist consultant. Offer a free pilot to 10 estate and elder-law firms through bar CLE lunches and local ACTEC chapters, targeting one blended-family client each. Aim for 5 paid sessions by day 30.

ideas.title: Critical-Error Benchmark for Legal Transcription AI
ideas.one_liner: An independent, reporter-built test suite that scores transcription AI on the errors that lose cases, such as dropped negatives, swapped numbers, wrong speaker and uh-huh versus huh-uh. Court and law-firm buyers pay for procurement reports, and vendors pay for certification.
ideas.customer: State court administrative offices and county courts running digital-recording or AI pilots. Large law firm innovation and procurement teams. Insurer litigation-management groups. The AI transcription vendors themselves, who buy a certification badge.
ideas.problem: Every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy, measured as word error rate on clean audio. That metric treats 'I did not see him' becoming 'I did see him' as one wrong word in six, no worse than a dropped 'the.' Reporters know the real failure points: negations, numbers (fifteen versus fifty), proper names, speaker attribution in crosstalk, uh-huh versus huh-uh, soft-spoken witnesses, and interpreted testimony. Court procurement officers and firm buyers have no independent comparison, so RFPs copy vendor claims.
ideas.solution: Build a hidden test set from staged mock depositions and hearings. Working reporters play scripted witnesses and attorneys, recorded in courtroom reverb, on Zoom, with masks, accents and interpreters. Each recording has certified steno ground truth and annotated critical-error spans. Publish a Critical Error Rate per hour with per-category scores. Release a free public subset and leaderboard for credibility. Charge for private bake-offs on a buyer's own audio, graded by reporters. Sell annual certification with re-testing whenever a vendor updates its model.
ideas.why_now: Shortages are pushing courts to adopt digital and AI reporting, and Texas, North Dakota and California have all moved on it in different ways. The federal proposal for new Rule 707 signals that courts want reliability standards for machine output. Vendors are consolidating (Verbit owns Veritext). State court technology offices are writing RFPs now with no independent yardstick.
ideas.revenue_model: $15,000-$40,000 per court or firm procurement evaluation. $25,000-$75,000 per year per vendor for certification and re-testing. $3,000-$8,000 per year for benchmark subscription reports to firms and insurers. Licensing test sets to vendors under strict separation from the certification arm.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Accuracy is measured by the people selling it. The profession that produces legal ground truth for a living is the natural auditor. A dropped 'not' is the error class that ends careers in this field, and word error rate hides it as noise.
ideas.first_30_days: Hire 8 working reporters at $75-$100 per hour for weekend sessions. Produce 20 hours of staged audio and run 6 vendors. Publish a free 'Negation Error Report' that reporter associations will share. Email 15 state court technology officers and the National Center for State Courts. Offer each vendor a free re-test to start certification conversations.

ideas.title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
ideas.one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
ideas.customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
ideas.problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
ideas.solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.

ideas.title: Off-the-Record Governance for AI Meeting Transcripts
ideas.one_liner: A policy layer over Zoom, Teams and Meet notetakers that decides what becomes 'the record'. It auto-pauses for privileged talk, purges verbatim transcripts once counsel-approved minutes are certified, and blocks unauthorized bots.
ideas.customer: General counsel and compliance leads at regulated mid-market companies with 200-5,000 employees, such as healthcare systems, fintechs, biotechs and defense contractors. Also law firms and corporate secretaries who run board minutes.
ideas.problem: AI notetakers made every meeting a verbatim, discoverable and error-prone transcript by default. A wrong attribution, such as 'we knew' instead of 'we know,' can become an exhibit. Third-party bots joining privileged calls raise waiver risk. Recording-consent class actions against AI notetaker vendors are rising, especially in all-party-consent states. General counsel have no control primitive between 'record everything' and 'ban notetakers.'
ideas.solution: A meeting-level record mode with three states: on the record, off the record and privileged. It is enforced through calendar tags, participant signals (a lawyer joins, so transcript is suppressed) and admin APIs for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. Verbatim transcripts carry retention timers (7-30 days, unless a legal hold applies). A named human designee approves a summary, which becomes the sole record with an attestation stamp modeled on a reporter's certificate. Add an audit log and a bot allow-list. It sits on top of the notetakers the company already uses.
ideas.why_now: Enterprises spent 2025-26 rolling out Copilot, Gemini and Zoom AI notes company-wide. Lawsuits over AI notetaker recording consent were filed in 2025. Regulators have punished off-channel record-keeping failures, so record governance is now a board-level topic. Legal teams are asking for controls now.
ideas.revenue_model: $6-$12 per user per month with a $25,000 annual minimum. An entry 'Record Risk Audit' as a fixed $5,000-$10,000 project that converts to the platform. A channel through employment and litigation law firms that advise clients on AI policy.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Reporters live by one ritual, 'off the record,' a physical control (they stop writing) that AI notetakers lack. They also know that outside a proceeding a verbatim transcript is a liability, not an asset. Most companies are only now realizing they built a huge discoverable archive of casual speech.
ideas.first_30_days: Sell the $5,000 audit to 10 general counsel through ACC chapters and LinkedIn. Inventory each company's bot footprint from admin logs and deliver a policy template. Build a thin MVP using Microsoft Graph and Google admin APIs that flips transcription per meeting from calendar tags. Convert 3 audits into paid pilots.

ideas.title: Lot Vault: Reagent Warranty Claims and Lot Registry
ideas.one_liner: A photo-the-label app that files unclaimed reagent-guarantee refunds for labs, quietly builds the only lot-level reagent performance database, and then group-buys locked good lots for small labs.
ideas.customer: Lab managers and PIs in organoid, iPSC, primary-immune-cell and antibody-heavy labs (about $79-199/month per lab). Core facilities and departments with central purchasing pay for the site-wide tier. Later, challenger reagent vendors and distributors pay for lot-level analytics.
ideas.problem: Every experienced postdoc knows the hidden variable behind failed experiments is the reagent lot: FBS, Matrigel/BME, B27, human serum, antibodies, polymerases. A lot that passes the vendor's certificate of analysis can still kill your organoids, and nobody logs lot numbers. Vendors' satisfaction guarantees require the lot number, images and a claim inside a time window, so postdocs almost never file. Money goes unclaimed. Six labs across town hit the same bad lot and never find out. When a good lot runs out, a two-year experimental series has to be re-validated.
ideas.solution: Wedge: a phone app where the postdoc snaps the vial label and taps 'worked' or 'failed', with optional gel or blot photos. On 'failed' it drafts the vendor guarantee claim with lot, dates and images, and tracks the credit. On 'worked' it logs the lot against the user's cell type and assay. Over time this becomes a crowd-sourced registry: 'Matrigel lot X: 7 of 9 organoid labs report failure.' Phase 2: when a lot shows good in at least 5 labs, the company negotiates a vendor lot reservation and runs a pooled group buy. Small labs get a locked lot for 12-24 months without needing 100 bottles of freezer space. The company takes a 10-15% margin.
ideas.why_now: NIH funding disruption and higher reagent prices from tariffs (verify current tariff levels) make labs care about every wasted dollar in 2025-26. Vision LLMs make label OCR and claim drafting almost free. Reproducibility pressure is high and the NIH is pushing rigor. Vendors are consolidating, and challenger brands need a credible independent signal to displace incumbents.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription per lab or per core. A 10-15% margin on group-buy locked-lot sales. Success-fee or flat fee on recovered credits. Later, paid lot-analytics dashboards for challenger vendors and distributors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The certificate of analysis tests the vendor's assay, not yours. The only real lot-quality signal is 'the lab down the hall using my cell type', and that signal already circulates informally by hallway lore. Nobody has digitized it because no single lab has enough data. The warranty-claim refund is the Trojan horse: it gives the user immediate ROI, so people log lot numbers without being asked, and it produces the data moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a no-code MVP: a forwarding inbox plus a form that pulls lot number and catalog number and drafts claim emails. Recruit 15 labs from organoid and iPSC Slack and Discord channels and postdoc association lists. Offer 3 months free plus a 'we file it for you' concierge. File the first 30 claims by hand to learn each vendor's rules. Show each lab the dollars recovered. Convert to $99/month once the first credit lands. In parallel, pick one product (for example BME or FBS) and quote a pooled lot reservation to 10 pilot labs.

ideas.title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
ideas.one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
ideas.customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
ideas.problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
ideas.solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
ideas.why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose one subfield you personally have 20 contacts in (for example CAR-T, organoids, targeted protein degradation or spatial biology). Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.

ideas.title: Exchange for Shelved Academic Projects and Null Data
ideas.one_liner: Buy the 'graveyard' of academic labs, meaning abandoned projects, validated knockout lines, half-built assays and failed-experiment data, and resell them as dossiers with an interview slot to seed biotechs and AI-bio data teams. Supply is anchored by a paid lab-closure clearance service.
ideas.customer: Sellers: departing postdocs, PIs downsizing or closing labs, and department chairs and EHS offices who must clear the space. Buyers: seed biotech founders, AI-bio and virtual-cell model companies that need experimental data including null results, pharma target-validation groups, and CROs that need validated cell models. Dossiers sell for $3-30k, and closure concierge fees run $5-15k.
ideas.problem: Every lab has a graveyard: KO lines, reporter constructs, a half-optimized assay, a screen that didn't pan out, and boxes in the -80 labeled 'JK 3/14 P3 #2'. When a postdoc leaves or a lab shrinks, the physical items are discarded or become orphaned, and the reasons the project failed leave in the postdoc's head. Meanwhile a startup or AI-bio team pays 12 months and $500k to rebuild the same tools and rediscover the same dead ends. Published literature is heavily biased toward positives, and models trained only on positives are systematically overconfident.
ideas.solution: Two-sided wedge. Supply side: 'Lab Closure Concierge' is a fixed-fee triage service for labs that are closing or downsizing. It inventories freezers, plasmids, cell lines and mouse lines, interviews the departing postdoc for 90 minutes to capture provenance and failure reasons (transcribed and structured with AI), disposes of hazardous items compliantly, and flags what is worth keeping. Demand side: a curated catalog of 'dossiers': the physical or digital assets, protocols, raw data including nulls, plus a paid call with the person who built them. Use a standard institutional license or MTA template with a revenue share to the university, so overloaded tech-transfer offices approve it because the alternative is a dumpster.
ideas.why_now: NIH grant terminations, indirect-cost fights and uncertain 2026 budgets are pushing labs to shrink or close. Biotech shutdowns have also left surplus bench assets (verify current scale). AI-bio companies are openly short of high-quality experimental data, especially negative data, and pay for it. Tech-transfer offices are understaffed. LLM transcription and structuring turns a 90-minute interview into a searchable dossier cheaply.
ideas.revenue_model: Closure-concierge flat fee paid by the department or PI. A 25-30% commission on dossier sales, with revenue share to seller and institution. Annual data-subscription tier for AI-bio buyers (curated null-result feeds).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The vials are worth very little. The value is provenance plus the 'why it failed' story stored in one person's memory, and it evaporates the day the postdoc's visa or contract ends. So the product is not a marketplace for samples, it is structured exit-knowledge capture with a physical-asset appendix. Because the university owns the IP anyway, the clean structure is to make the institution a paid party rather than an obstacle.
ideas.first_30_days: Use your own postdoc network to line up 3-5 labs that are shrinking or have departing postdocs. Offer a free triage-and-catalog audit in exchange for permission to list a few assets. Produce 10 dossiers with structured interviews. Cold-email 30 seed biotechs and AI-bio data leads with the top 5 dossiers. Close one sale at $3-8k. Use that transaction to test the university revenue-share template with one tech-transfer office.

ideas.title: Night-Shift Bench Techs for Time-Critical Experiments
ideas.one_liner: An agency of vetted, laid-off bench technicians who show up at 2 a.m. or on Christmas morning to harvest time points, feed cells and load overnight runs from the lab's own protocol cards, with photo proof and a break-glass line to the postdoc.
ideas.customer: Small private biotechs and startups in shared lab space (LabCentral-type incubators and coworking labs), plus soft-money academic labs with reagent or staffing budgets and industry-funded academic labs. Billed at $85-120/hour with a 2-hour minimum. The incubator or landlord earns a referral fee.
ideas.problem: Biology runs on its own clock. 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. time-course harvests, weekend and holiday cell feeding, 48-hour induction windows and overnight instrument runs are the hidden cost of every wet-lab career. Postdocs cover them with sleep debt, guilt-based favors from grad students, or driving in on Christmas. The person who could do it is often laid off, but a lab will not hand $40k of iPSC-derived cells to a stranger, and access badges and insurance make casual help impossible.
ideas.solution: A W-2 (employer-of-record) pool of experienced techs, aseptic-technique certified and proven on a practice run, working from the customer's 'protocol cards'. Each shift is a fixed product: Time-Point Harvest, Weekend Split and Feed, Holiday Cover, Overnight Run Loader. Each has a checklist, timestamped photos at every step, a pre-shift 30-minute video walkthrough, and a break-glass contact. Sitters first do a 'dry run' on the customer's cheap spare line. Incubator and coworking-lab operators put the agency on an approved-vendor list, which solves badge and insurance access once for hundreds of labs.
ideas.why_now: A large pool of experienced bench techs and postdocs has been released by biotech layoffs since 2023 and funding disruption in 2025-26. Lean startups have fewer people per experiment, so time-critical work lands on founders. Bigger time-course, organoid and perturbation experiments driven by AI-bio data demand make odd-hour work more frequent. Shared-lab operators want more amenities to fill vacant benches.
ideas.revenue_model: A markup on billed hours (techs are paid about $40-55/hour, the agency bills $85-120). Monthly retainer for guaranteed availability (for example 'holiday cover pass'). Referral revenue share from shared-lab operators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The hard constraint is trust, not skill. Nobody outsources their cells because failure is invisible until weeks later. So the product is really an evidence-and-liability wrapper: photo proof, protocol cards, dry runs, and operator pre-approval. Also, the early customers are not academia (IACUC, badges and university procurement kill it) but private benches in rented lab space, where one operator agreement unlocks dozens of labs.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 recently laid-off techs through personal networks and biotech alumni groups. Get a business license, a staffing or PEO partner for payroll, and general liability insurance. Call the community managers at 2-3 shared-lab spaces in one city and offer the first holiday-cover week free. Sell the first paid 3 a.m. harvest to a founder who is already doing it themselves. Turn every job into a reusable protocol card. Aim for about 10 recurring customers by month 6.

ideas.title: Cryo-Vault for Artisan Food Microbial Cultures
ideas.one_liner: Backup-and-rescue service that fingerprints, isolates and cryo-banks the living house cultures (cheese rind flora, koji, kombucha SCOBYs, sourdough starters, mushroom spawn, natural-wine yeast) of small food producers in split-geography -80 storage, with a 48-hour emergency revival.
ideas.customer: Small artisan producers: raw-milk and farmstead cheesemakers, koji, miso and sake makers, kombucha brewers, specialty mushroom growers, sourdough bakeries, natural winemakers and cideries. Pay $250-400 intake plus $20-40/month per culture, and $400-600 per emergency rescue.
ideas.problem: A small producer's house culture is their product identity, yet it lives on the counter or in a single fridge, propagated by serial subculture. Mother cultures senesce and drift, contaminate, or get wiped out by phage (dairy) or Trichoderma-type molds (mushrooms). One crash can end a brand for months. Big culture houses won't bank a small producer's strains, and commercial biobank services are priced and designed for pharma.
ideas.solution: A mail-in kit: send a gram of culture, get back an ITS/16S-based composition fingerprint, viability and purity report, and isolated key strains. Each is banked as glycerol stocks in triplicate at two separate sites, with a dashboard of banked cultures. The rescue tier revives a viable working culture in 48 hours with contamination diagnosis, and later adds a periodic 'drift check' compared against the banked baseline. Optional fingerprint certificates for craft-authenticity claims and geographic-indication programs.
ideas.why_now: Fermentation and koji-based craft food is booming, and sequencing costs are trivial (about $30 per amplicon sample). Consolidation and climate stress are raising the cost of a culture crash. Small food makers increasingly market on 'living' and heritage claims that they can't currently back up. Laid-off microbiologists can staff this cheaply.
ideas.revenue_model: Intake fee plus recurring monthly vault subscription per culture. Per-event rescue fees. Fingerprint certificates and drift-check add-ons. Later B2B with food-safety consultants and craft trade associations, which bundle it as a member benefit.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Cryo-banking with a genetic fingerprint is routine bench hygiene for any wet-lab, but the food world has never been offered it at a price small producers can pay. Nobody thinks of 'my sourdough' as a strain to back up until it crashes. The wedge is not the science, it is the packaging as insurance and the rescue promise.
ideas.first_30_days: Bank 10 cultures for free from friendly producers (cheesemakers, kombucha and mushroom growers) recruited through guild forums and Facebook groups. Rent -80 space at a university core, a co-lab or a local biobank. Use a commercial amplicon sequencing service for fingerprints. Publish one story about a rescued culture. Convert the first cohort to $99/month founding-member pricing. Stay strictly with BSL-1 food-grade organisms and set clear policies on pathogen refusal and shipping.

ideas.title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
ideas.one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
ideas.customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
ideas.problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
ideas.solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
ideas.why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
ideas.revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.

ideas.title: Cross-Landlord Fake-Employer and Fake-Reference Registry
ideas.one_liner: A shared network that spots rental fraud by the out-of-band details forgers cannot fake, such as the same 'HR' phone number, burner line or 'previous landlord' reused across dozens of leasing offices.
ideas.customer: Independent and mid-size property managers (50 to 5,000 units) who process applications themselves and lack a fraud team. They pay per application or per portfolio. Later customers are auto lenders, buy-here-pay-here dealers, gig-work platforms and small-balance mortgage lenders, who all verify employers and references the same way.
ideas.problem: Application fraud is now professional. The pay stubs, bank statements and offer letters are fabricated, and the 'employer' is a shell whose 'HR line' is answered by an accomplice. Even the 'previous landlord' reference is a friend. Every leasing office catches one of these files, throws it out, and never tells anyone. The same ring then applies at the property across town and eventually gets a lease. The eviction that follows costs $8,000 to $20,000 and several months. Document-forensics tools catch sloppy Photoshop, but once image generators can produce perfect pay stubs (as they now can), the lie is no longer in the PDF. It is in the phone number and the employer that do not exist.
ideas.solution: An API and browser extension for leasing staff. Staff enter the employer name, HR phone or email, the previous-landlord contact and the stated address. The system returns a risk read built from three signals. First, telecom line-type and age (VoIP or burner, number recently ported or activated). Second, business-registry and domain checks (EIN, formation date, mismatched address, brand-new domain). Third, and this is the moat, network signals: how many distinct applicants at how many unrelated landlords used this exact phone, email, employer or landlord reference in the last 12 months, and whether any of those files were confirmed fraud by a participating PM. Participants contribute confirmed-fraud entities and get read access, and entries link to entities (phones, domains, businesses), not to named individuals. That design keeps most of the data outside consumer-report regulation, and any person-linked entry gets a dispute and correction workflow.
ideas.why_now: Generative image models make forged financial documents indistinguishable in 2025 and 2026, which pushes the defensive signal from document pixels to out-of-band verification. Fraud-detection vendors for leasing are consolidating around documents, so an entity-level shared registry sits in the gap. Large PMs have internal fraud teams, and the long tail of independents has nothing. Rental markets that are softer with more concessions also attract more fraud-ring activity aimed at free-rent giveaways and quick move-ins.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.50 to $3.00 per application check, or $149 to $499 per month by portfolio size with a contribution-based discount. Enterprise API licensing to lenders and platforms later. Data-contribution credits make the network self-seeding.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rental fraud rings reuse infrastructure across landlords far more than they reuse identities. The same 'HR' number answers for 14 different companies. But no single landlord sees more than one or two, so the pattern is invisible without a network. It works like ISO ClaimSearch did for insurance claims. Because the registry tracks entities and not people, it sidesteps most of the fair-lending and consumer-reporting objections that killed earlier landlord blacklists.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 PMs from local NARPM chapters and landlord Facebook groups. Ask each to send the last 20 to 50 confirmed-fraud files (phone, email, employer, reference only, no SSNs), and seed the database from those. Run the pooled data for overlaps and show each PM how many of their 'unique' fraudsters overlapped with someone else's. Ship a Chrome extension that checks a phone or email against the database plus Twilio Lookup. Free for the first 60 days for contributors, then $149 per month. Have a fair-credit-reporting attorney review the entity-only design and the dispute process before charging.

ideas.title: Inherited-Rental Stabilization Service for Estate Attorneys
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee 30-day service that stabilizes rental properties the moment an owner dies, sold through probate attorneys and trust officers who fear personal liability.
ideas.customer: Probate and trust-and-estates attorneys, professional fiduciaries and bank trust departments who represent executors and heirs of deceased small landlords. Attorney or fiduciary pays the flat fee out of the estate. Beneficiaries later pay ongoing management or sale-prep fees.
ideas.problem: The average small landlord is in their 60s or older, and a wave of these owners is dying and passing on 2-to-30-unit portfolios to heirs who have never landlorded. In the first 60 to 90 days after death everything degrades. Tenants get confused about who to pay and some quietly stop, so collections drop 20 to 40%. The named insured on the policy is dead and coverage gets contested or non-renewed. Security deposits, a legal liability that has to be accounted for in trust, are mingled into the deceased's personal account. Leases are undocumented handshake month-to-months, and vendors stop being paid. The attorney does not want to run a rental business but is exposed to a beneficiary surcharge claim if value leaks.
ideas.solution: A productized 'Day-1 Stabilization Package' delivered by a small field team and software. It has five parts. First, a tenant estoppel and 'pay here' notice with a new rent-collection account, sent within 5 days. Second, a rent-roll and lease audit, verifying every tenant, deposit and lease term against bank records. Third, deposit-liability reconciliation and a segregated trust account. Fourth, insurance re-papering: new named-insured and vacancy status filings. Fifth, a code-compliance and deferred-maintenance walk-through, with photos, for the estate inventory and stepped-up-basis appraisal support. The output is a court-ready fiduciary report the attorney can file. The last step is an option: convert to ongoing management at a preferential rate, or a sale-ready package for listing.
ideas.why_now: The great wealth transfer from boomers is reaching real estate now, and small individual landlords are among the oldest owner cohorts. Rising property values make each estate's rental portfolio high-stakes. Attorneys are reluctant to run operating businesses, and fiduciary surcharge risk is well understood. Large PM firms ignore 6-unit estates. Cloud rent collection and e-sign tools make a 30-day remote-plus-local process feasible for a tiny team.
ideas.revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,000 flat fee per estate (scaled by unit count), paid by the estate. About 30 to 40% of estates convert into ongoing management at 7 to 9% of rent, or into a listing or sale referral with a 1 to 2% fee. Bank trust departments can be sold an annual retainer.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The best property-management clients are never won through marketing. They arrive through a death, and the person deciding who gets the call is an attorney who cares about liability, not price or software features. The attorney's real product need is documentation to defend against beneficiary surcharge claims, not better rent collection. The real revenue leak in the first 90 days is the 'ghost landlord' period, when tenants do not know who to pay.
ideas.first_30_days: Write the checklist and notice templates (a weekend of work if you have PM experience). Contact 30 probate attorneys and 5 corporate fiduciary or trust officers in one metro, offering a free 45-minute CLE-style talk on 'the first 90 days of an inherited rental portfolio' through the county bar's trusts and estates section. Offer a discounted first stabilization at cost to two attorneys for testimonials and case studies. Line up a bookkeeper and a local handyman for the field-work side and use existing PM software for rent collection.

ideas.title: Abandoned Property and Tenant-Death Response Crew
ideas.one_liner: A per-event service that handles the legally dangerous moments landlords dread most, such as a tenant who vanishes leaving belongings or a tenant who dies alone, with statutory clocks, next-of-kin outreach and documented disposal.
ideas.customer: Property managers and small landlords, who pay per event ($400 to $1,500). Later customers are eldercare social workers, hospital discharge teams, medical examiners' offices and estate attorneys, who all need someone to close out a residence properly.
ideas.problem: A 400-unit manager deals with a handful of abandonments a year and one to three tenant deaths. Each event is handled ad hoc. Abandoned-property statutes vary by state, with notice periods, itemized inventory rules, value thresholds and sale-or-storage requirements. One mistake, such as tossing a bin or entering too early, creates conversion or wrongful-eviction liability. With a death, no one has authority to enter or dispose of belongings, the estate has no representative yet, next of kin are unknown or hostile, rent accrues, and the unit sits dark for months. Hoarding and biohazard situations make it worse. There is no standard vendor, so the maintenance supervisor is doing legal and emotional work no one trained him for.
ideas.solution: A regional response team with a state-specific statutory workflow. Step one is intake and legal-clock software, which starts the required notice dates, produces the notices, photo-inventory and valuation report and stores it as evidence. Step two is next-of-kin and estate-representative outreach, with sensitivity training for the caller. Step three is secure storage in a partner facility, then sale, donation or disposal exactly as the statute allows, with receipts. Step four is coordinating hoarding or biohazard remediation and the final walk-through for deposit accounting. A companion product is an e-signable lease addendum letting tenants (especially seniors) name an emergency contact and authorized person for post-death property disposition, in the states where that is permitted. That builds a pipeline of pre-authorized cases and makes each later event simple.
ideas.why_now: The number of renters aged 65+ living alone is growing fast, which means more deaths in rental units and more hoarding and welfare issues. Several states have recently added or modernized tenant-designated-contact and abandoned-property procedures, though rules remain patchy. Software-only proptech has ignored this because it is field work. Junk-removal and storage marketplaces have made the physical logistics cheap to subcontract.
ideas.revenue_model: $400 to $1,500 flat fee per abandonment or death event, plus pass-through storage and disposal cost at a 15 to 25% markup. Optional readiness subscription ($1 to $2 per unit per month) for PMs, covering the lease addendum, templates and priority response. Eldercare and estate-attorney referral relationships add a second channel.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Ordinary landlords fear the eviction. Experienced managers fear the abandonment and the death, because the law in those cases punishes shortcuts, no procedure exists, and the loss (months of rent plus liability) is bigger than a normal eviction. Nobody sells the service because each case is small and the required knowledge is a stack of 50 state statutes. That fragmentation is the moat: once you have playbooks for a handful of states, competitors cannot copy them quickly.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state and read the abandoned-property and death-of-tenant statutes closely, ideally with a landlord-tenant attorney on a fixed-fee review. Build the notice, inventory and timeline templates. Sign three PMs (find them through the local NARPM or apartment association) to a pilot: 'call us on the next event, first one at cost'. Line up a junk-removal company, a storage unit partner and a biohazard remediation subcontractor. Publish a simple blog page and a landlord-association talk titled 'What to do when a tenant dies or disappears' to start inbound.

ideas.title: Listing Bodyguard: Scam-Listing Takedown for Property Managers
ideas.one_liner: Continuously scans the web for scam copies of a property manager's listings and takes them down, and gives real prospects a fast way to verify that a listing is legitimate.
ideas.customer: Property managers and leasing companies with 100 to 3,000 units, paying a monthly subscription. The buyer is the marketing or leasing director. Secondary buyers are apartment associations, large landlords' insurers and rental listing portals.
ideas.problem: Scammers copy a manager's real listing photos, undercut the rent by 25 to 40% and collect application fees and deposits from victims who never see the unit. Victims then show up at the property or call the leasing office furious, and often leave one-star reviews of the real manager. Real leads are poached by the fake listing, and the leasing team wastes hours on angry callers and manual takedown requests to Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace and others. There is no owner of the problem: the listing platforms are slow, police shrug and the PM's syndication vendor does not monitor. AI now makes it trivial to generate thousands of fake listings, with photos rewritten and descriptions localized.
ideas.solution: Pull each PM's live listing feed (from the syndication export in AppFolio, Buildium, Yardi or RentManager), compute perceptual hashes of every photo and fingerprints of the description text and address, then continuously search for matches across Craigslist, Zillow-family sites, Facebook (through allowed methods and user reports), OfferUp and the open web through reverse-image APIs. When a match appears on a listing whose contact does not belong to the PM, the system files takedown requests through each platform's copyright, fraud or impersonation channel with evidence, tracks status, and escalates. Prevention layer: every real listing gets a short verification code ('Verify: text 4471 to our verified line'), and a landing page confirms the unit and the real contact, giving prospects a free way to check before wiring money. Weekly reports show scams blocked, leads protected and estimated victim exposure.
ideas.why_now: Generative AI made scam listings cheap and scalable in 2025 and 2026, and consumer-protection agencies continue to list rental scams among the top fraud categories. Rental portals are under pressure to verify but are slow. The reverse-image and vision APIs from major providers make similarity search inexpensive, and the takedown channels are already documented, so a small team can automate a job that leasing staff currently do by hand.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.50 to $1.50 per active listing per month with a $199 monthly minimum, or a flat tier for portfolios. Upsell: white-label verification pages and analytics for apartment associations, and API licensing to listing portals and insurers who want fewer fraud claims.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: To a leasing office, a scam listing is not a consumer-fraud story. It is a top-of-funnel leak and a brand problem, because the scammer steals real leads and the victims blame the PM. Managers already know this but treat it as a nuisance, so there is a budget for a fix but no product. The real moat is the takedown playbook per platform: which channel, which wording, which contact person actually gets a listing removed within hours rather than days.
ideas.first_30_days: Manually audit 3 to 5 friendly PMs: take their public listings, run reverse-image searches and show them the scam copies already live (there will be some). That audit is the sales pitch, and most PMs have never looked. Build a script using Google Vision web-detection or TinEye plus Craigslist and Marketplace searches for a first pass, and a shared dashboard for takedown status. Charge $199 per month per portfolio starting in month 2. Ask each PM for a testimonial and a 'stopped 14 scams last quarter' number to bring to the next landlord association talk.

ideas.title: Fresh-Address Desk for Medicaid Plans
ideas.one_liner: Turn Title I front offices into a consent-based channel that keeps families on Medicaid, paid per household retained by health plans and hospitals, with a revenue share to the school.
ideas.customer: Medicaid managed care plans (member retention and quality-bonus teams) and nonprofit hospitals with community-benefit budgets. Principals and PTAs are the channel partners and receive a revenue share. They do not pay.
ideas.problem: Six-month renewals and work-requirement paperwork are scheduled to hit expansion-adult Medicaid enrollees in 2027. Plans lose members when renewal mail goes to old addresses and phone numbers, and their call-center contact rates are dismal. Kids often lose coverage in the household churn even when they stay eligible. Plans cannot reach the families who most need help, and the parent hears the plan's mail as junk.
ideas.solution: A text-first, home-language 'update your info and check your renewal' flow built into the school's existing August packet and registration. A part-time parent-liaison 'benefits desk' sits in the front office a few hours a week. Data goes to a plan only with a signed opt-in parent consent, not under FERPA directory information. Plans pay a fee per verified address or phone update and per completed renewal. About 30 percent of the revenue goes to a school-controlled discretionary fund. The same desk later handles other bounty-paying programs: utility low-income enrollment, Lifeline phone and internet plans, Summer EBT, and vision and dental follow-up.
ideas.why_now: Under the 2025 budget reconciliation law, expansion-adult redeterminations move to every 6 months after the end of 2026 and work requirements begin in 2027, unless states get a delay. The post-COVID Medicaid unwinding showed that most coverage losses were procedural. Principals are also hungry for discretionary dollars after the 2025 federal freezes and cancelled school-mental-health grants.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-household bounty of roughly $25 to $75 for a verified update or completed renewal. Plans also pay an annual per-school or per-region program fee. Optional add-on bounties from utilities and phone carriers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The freshest address and phone database of low-income families is not held by any agency. It is held by the school secretary, who re-verifies it every August because busing, lunch and emergency cards depend on it. Families ignore the plan's letters but answer the office they trust. Principals will only say yes if the money flows back to the school and consent is explicit, and that design is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state and call the community-engagement or quality director at two or three Medicaid plans. Offer a 90-day pilot in 3 schools whose principals you already know, priced per verified update. Build it with Twilio and a bilingual part-timer, and use a hashed list-match to show how many of a plan's returned-mail members appear in school records. Have the principal co-sign a one-page consent form that PTA volunteers can hand out.

ideas.title: Audit-Proof Family Night in a Box
ideas.one_liner: Fixed-price, compliance-packaged family engagement events for Title I schools, paid from the federally required parent-engagement set-aside, with the monitoring binder as the real product.
ideas.customer: District Title I coordinators and Title I principals. The money comes from the ESSA parent and family engagement reserve, which is 1 percent of Title I for districts above the size threshold, and most of it must go to schools.
ideas.problem: That money is earmarked but scary to spend. Principals fear audit findings over food, childcare, transport, interpreters and incentives, because each has 'necessary and reasonable' tests and must tie back to the district's engagement policy and the school-parent compact. Events get thin turnout of 20 to 30 percent of families. Principals end up buying pizza with sketchy funds, or the money sits unspent until spring.
ideas.solution: A fully produced event in a box. It is built around students performing or presenting, and includes a dinner from a local caterer, on-site childcare, ride vouchers, live interpreters and a personal invitation call script. Every event ships with a pre-vetted allowable-cost memo, an agenda tied to the compact and policy, QR sign-in, a parent needs survey, an evaluation report and a monitoring-ready binder generated automatically. Packages are $4.5k to $9k per event, with annual bundles for a district.
ideas.why_now: After the July 2025 federal funding freeze scare and post-ESSER budget cuts, coordinators are under pressure to spend every Title I dollar on time and defensibly. Chronic absenteeism has stuck near one in four students, and family engagement is the best-evidenced lever schools have left. States are also stepping up monitoring of federal-funds documentation.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-event fixed fee ($4.5k to $9k), annual multi-event contracts ($25k to $60k per school), and a district-wide compliance template license.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Turnout comes from four things nobody bundles: kids on stage, food, childcare in the building, and a personal call from a known adult. The real blocker is not attendance. It is the principal's fear of an audit finding, so the binder is what they are buying and the event is only the delivery vehicle. Vendors that sell 'parent engagement software' miss this because the software cannot make an allowable-cost decision.
ideas.first_30_days: Read one state's Title I monitoring protocol and write a two-page allowable-cost memo. Get two Title I coordinators to comment on it and agree to a template. Pitch 5 principals you know, and run 3 pilot events at cost with a local caterer and a bilingual emcee. Capture turnout data versus the school's usual events. Turn the paperwork into a reusable binder generator.

ideas.title: Turn Half-Empty School Wings Into Child Care
ideas.one_liner: A turnkey operator that leases empty classrooms in half-empty Title I elementary schools and runs licensed infant, toddler and before/after-school care in them.
ideas.customer: School districts that lease the space (landlord side). Revenue comes from parents (including those on state child-care subsidies), state pre-K funds, and employers or the district itself buying slots for staff.
ideas.problem: Birth-rate decline has left many elementary schools 20 to 40 percent empty, and districts are closing buildings.
