Yet the neighborhood has no infant care, teachers quit over child care, and before/after-school waitlists run for months. Empty rooms cost the district no visible money, so nobody champions them, and district counsel treats a sublease as a liability risk.
ideas.solution: Sell a feasibility and licensing audit ($5k to $15k) covering egress, restrooms, square footage per child, fencing, a separate entrance, and the fire marshal. Then operate the program as a license-holding subtenant. Staff it with cross-trained paras and neighborhood parents. Accept subsidy vouchers and state pre-K slots. Give priority to school staff and Title I families, and keep before- and after-school care in the same building. The district gets rent plus a utilities share, and the operator keeps a thin margin.
ideas.why_now: Enrollment declines and school-closure fights are peaking. The 2025 tax law raised the employer child-care tax credit starting in 2026, which helps districts and employers underwrite staff slots. Several states are expanding subsidized or universal child care. Federal after-school funding uncertainty in 2025 also opened a gap for paid programs.
ideas.revenue_model: Tuition and subsidy revenue for the operator. One-time feasibility and licensing fees. Optional management fee if a nonprofit or district holds the license.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone talks about reusing closed schools. The money is in schools that stay open but are half-empty, where a wing can be subleased tomorrow with no rezoning. Elementary buildings already meet many child-care code items: kid-height restrooms, exits, a playground and a kitchen. The principal knows this from living in the building. The blocker is the district's lease template and its fear of liability, and both are solvable with paperwork.
ideas.first_30_days: Map licensing rules in one state and find a nonprofit child-care operator willing to hold the license. Pitch 5 superintendents and principals with a two-page space-utilization audit and a sample lease. Sell three $5k feasibility audits to fund the pilot, and use waitlists from existing before/after-school programs as proof of demand.

ideas.title: Paid Neighbor Walking Routes for Absent Kids
ideas.one_liner: Hire retired neighbors and parents as paid 'route captains' who walk or wake up chronically absent kids on fixed blocks, and get paid a share of the funding that the recovered attendance brings back.
ideas.customer: Principals and districts in states that fund schools on average daily attendance (California, Texas and similar). Secondary payers are city safe-passage budgets, Title I funds and Medicaid plans (for asthma and chronic-condition kids).
ideas.problem: About one in four kids is chronically absent. Nudge letters and text campaigns work on the 10 to 19 day group but barely touch the kids missing 25 or more days. For them it is a 7:40 a.m. logistics problem: a parent working an early shift, an older sibling who moved on to middle school, a dangerous corner, no clean clothes, no alarm clock. In attendance-funded states, each absent day costs the school roughly what a day of instruction is worth, so a $200-per-kid fix pays back several times over.
ideas.solution: Micro-employ 3 to 5 route captains per school as part-time W-2 workers (7:00 to 8:30 a.m., roughly $18 an hour). Each captain covers a block-by-block route, walking 6 to 10 kids, knocking on doors, and running a breakfast and laundry pass. Captains report barrier codes by voice note, which feed the attendance team's dashboard. Contract as a base route fee plus 20 to 25 percent of documented funding gains from improved attendance.
ideas.why_now: Chronic absenteeism has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. ESSER-funded attendance staff were cut as that money expired. States now require chronic-absence plans, and the retiree and gig-worker labor pool is looking for short, local, part-time work.
ideas.revenue_model: Base fee per route plus a performance share of recovered attendance funding. Optional per-route sponsorship from health plans or employers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Districts spend on software and letters, but the students who cost the most are the ones for whom the 7:40 a.m. logistics fail. The cheapest fix is a grandmother on the corner, and it is invisible to edtech buyers because it is not a product. The first three Mondays of September predict the year, so contracting has to start before October.
ideas.first_30_days: Pilot with one principal in an attendance-funded state: 2 routes, about 12 kids, 4 part-time captains recruited from churches and senior centers. Establish baselines from last year's attendance data and track days present weekly. Write the performance addendum as a one-page contract that a principal can sign with discretionary funds and later convert to a district contract.

ideas.title: Cash-Flow Lifeline for K-12 Service Vendors
ideas.one_liner: Same-week invoice funding for small vendors who serve schools (after-school, tutoring, therapy, van companies), priced using each district's known payment calendar, with a service-continuity guarantee for principals.
ideas.customer: Small K-12 vendors paying a financing fee: after-school providers, contract speech, occupational and counseling practices, tutoring companies, small van and transportation contractors, and arts and PE providers. Principals are the sponsor and the free channel.
ideas.problem: Districts pay invoices 60 to 120 days late, and federal-grant reimbursements (21st Century, Title programs) lag further. Small vendors run out of cash and vanish in October, mid-year, leaving kids without services. Principals cannot legally pay faster and get blamed when the therapist stops coming. Generic factoring companies price district risk like a private customer or refuse it.
ideas.solution: Fund invoices within 48 hours at 90 percent advance. Verification is a text or QR 'services delivered' confirmation from the principal, which is the step district accounts payable needs anyway. Price risk using each district's board-approval calendar, warrant runs and reimbursement cycles, which we assemble from public board minutes. Add a continuity guarantee: if a funded vendor fails, a pre-vetted bench vendor steps in. Districts get a simple notice-of-assignment form to sign.
ideas.why_now: The July 2025 withholding of roughly $6.8B in federal education funds, released weeks later, showed how fragile the timing is. Post-ESSER budgets are tight, and small-business credit is harder for vendors with slow government customers. LLMs can now read board packets, purchase orders and approval calendars at scale to predict pay dates.
ideas.revenue_model: Fee of about 1.5 to 3 percent per invoice per 30 days advanced, plus a vendor subscription ($99 per month) for the delivery-confirmation and invoicing workflow.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: District default risk is near zero. The risk is timing, and timing is predictable if you know how boards and warrant runs work. The principal's confirmation, not the bank, is the bottleneck, so whoever owns that step owns the data. Investors dismiss K-12 as slow and poor, but the payer is a taxing authority, which is the safest receivable there is.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 small vendors from principals' and coordinators' contact lists, starting with after-school and therapy contractors that have already had payment problems. Raise $150k to $300k of angel or warehouse capital and fund the first invoices at a flat fee. Build the district payment calendars in a spreadsheet from public minutes, which becomes the pricing model and the data moat.
